nodes.title: Feature Request: Multi-tenancy through dynamic bindings
nodes.body:
I am looking to manage multiple independent sites from a single EmDash installation/monorepo. Currently, EmDash appears focused on single-instance deployments. For devs managing dozens of client sites/properties, maintaining separate deployments for each site increases DevOps overhead and complicates global updates.

I would like to see native multi-tenancy support (similar to Payload CMS), allowing a single EmDash instance to:

- Identify tenants via domain name or request headers.

- Isolate data using either a shared database with tenantID scoping or separate D1 databases per tenant.

- Shared Codebase: Update the core CMS logic in one place (the monorepo/Worker) and have it reflect across all tenant sites immediately.

- Tenant-specific Configuration: Allow different themes or plugin settings based on the active tenant.

nodes.title: SchemaSmith v2.1.0 — one package, every schema (Schema Templates land)
nodes.body:
You've got fifty tenants, each in its own schema, the same tables in every one. So you copy the package fifty times, or you hand-roll a loop, or you deploy them one at a time and hope nothing drifts.

That's the job v2.1.0 takes off your plate.

**Schema Templates — multi-schema fan-out.** Write the schema once; SchemaQuench quenches it into every schema in a database. A `SchemaIdentificationScript` finds the targets, `{{SchemaName}}` flows into your scripts and JSON, and one canonical package deploys to all of them. Each tenant owns their schema; you own one definition. Need per-environment tenant rosters? `Target.TemplateTargets` drives the fan-out from settings and provisions missing schemas (and databases) for you. One package. Every environment. No forks.

That's the headline. Here's the rest of what landed:

- **Per-environment folder deployment** — put a `ShouldApplyExpression` on a whole script folder. A `MariaDB/` folder gated on `@@version`, a `Jobs/` folder skipped on Azure SQL, `TestData/` kept out of prod. Declarative, not pipeline branching.
- **Per-script runtime skip** — when only the script itself can decide whether it should run, raise the `SCHEMASMITH: SHOULD NOT APPLY` sentinel. SchemaQuench logs the skip and moves on. No failed deploy.
- **Log hygiene** — passwords, secrets, and connection strings get masked in the logs that end up in CI artifacts and support tickets. On by default, tunable.
- **Resolved-SQL artifact on failure** — when a script fails, the exact token-expanded SQL the server rejected is written to a re-runnable file, with the path right in the log. One open and you're looking at what actually ran.
- Plus `VariantName` labels for conditional variants, conditional full-text index variants on SQL Server, and a solid pile of fixes.

**Upgrading:** one breaking change — `Template.Required` is now `RequireAtLeastOneTarget` (clearer name, same behavior). Find-and-replace `"Required":` → `"RequireAtLeastOneTarget":` in your `Template.json` files and you're current. Everything else is additive.

Release notes: https://github.com/Schema-Smith/SchemaSmith/releases/tag/v2.1.0 · CHANGELOG: https://github.com/Schema-Smith/SchemaSmith/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md · upgrade with `choco upgrade schemasmith` (once moderation clears) or the `install.sh` one-liner.

Now the question I actually want answered: **how are you carving up your multi-tenant databases?** Schema-per-tenant, database-per-tenant, or one shared schema with a tenant column? Schema Templates is built for the schema-per-tenant crowd — I want to know if it fits how you actually work, or where it doesn't. Drop a reply.

Shape. Strengthen. Succeed.
— Forge

nodes.title: Hosted Storage Standard Upload: supported finality check after a lost response?
nodes.body:
We need to reconcile an already admitted Standard Upload during account erasure on hosted Supabase Storage.

Our application records an attempt before sending the upload, reserves a unique object path, uses upsert:false, and blocks new application writes when erasure begins. Consider this sequence:

1. A Standard Upload request is accepted, but the client loses its response.
2. The application stops issuing new uploads for that account.
3. A cleanup worker needs to know whether that earlier request can still commit or recreate the object after cleanup.

Is there a supported hosted API, operation identifier, cancellation/drain acknowledgment, or documented terminal-state guarantee that settles that earlier request? If there is no supported mechanism, please confirm that limitation explicitly.

The Storage reliability article describes cancellation of in-flight Postgres queries when a client disconnects. Does this provide an end-to-end guarantee for the object backend and any upload-completion work, or only for those database queries?

We are not treating an absent object in HEAD/list, a client-side abort, or elapsed time as proof that the earlier request cannot commit. We are also not claiming this is a reproduced product bug. We need the supported contract for hosted Standard Upload and guidance for reconciling already admitted requests; changing the protocol for future uploads would not by itself settle those old attempts.

References:
- https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/uploads/standard-uploads
- https://supabase.com/blog/supabase-storage-performance-security-reliability-updates

Please distinguish storage-object finality from CDN cache invalidation and retained backups, whose lifecycle we track separately.

nodes.title: Wheels 4.0 — multi-tenancy as a framework feature
nodes.body:
Multi-tenancy in 4.0 is in the framework, not in a plugin or community package. This post walks through the seam framing, how per-request datasource switching composes with the rest of the framework, the three deployment models supported, the deliberate escape hatches, and how 4.0 differs from the Rails / Laravel / Django approaches.

## Multi-tenancy is a seam problem

You need exactly one seam that catches every query, every job, every background task. Miss one — the straggler query in a report action, the `CreateObject("java", ...)` that goes around the ORM, the background job enqueued from a request that never asked whose tenant it was — and customer A sees customer B's invoice on a Sunday afternoon.

Plugin-based tenancy catches about eighty percent of the data paths. The hard twenty percent only gets caught when the seam lives below the consumer code, in the framework itself.

## How resolution works

[#1951](https://github.com/wheels-dev/wheels/pull/1951) — per-request datasource switching at the framework core. A tenant resolver runs in middleware before the controller instantiates. The resolved tenant attaches to the request, and the datasource resolver picks it up.

```cfm
// config/settings.cfm
set(middleware = [new app.middleware.TenantResolver()]);

// app/middleware/TenantResolver.cfc
component implements="wheels.middleware.MiddlewareInterface" {
    public any function handle(required struct request, required any next) {
        var subdomain = ListFirst(arguments.request.cgi.server_name, ".");
        arguments.request.tenant = subdomain;
        $setTenantDatasource(arguments.request.tenant);
        return arguments.next(arguments.request);
    }
}
```

The resolution source is up to you: subdomain (`acme.myapp.com`), path prefix (`/t/acme`), request header (`X-Tenant: acme`), or a claim out of a JWT (`tid`). Same middleware contract — pull the identifier, call `$setTenantDatasource`, pass the request along.

## Three SaaS data patterns supported

You pick by isolation requirement, not by framework limit.

- **Separate database per tenant** — cleanest isolation. Per-customer backup and restore, per-customer performance tuning, per-customer encryption at rest. The datasource resolver switches the entire connection per request. GDPR erasure is a `DROP DATABASE` away from complete.
- **Shared database, separate schema** — supported via datasource naming. One physical database, one connection pool, logical separation through schema prefixes. Middle ground between operational simplicity and isolation.
- **Shared database, row-level** — every table gets a `tenantId` column and every query gets scoped. Wheels supports it via default scopes, but this model requires the most discipline regardless of framework. The framework can't protect you from a hand-rolled join that forgets the where clause.

## Why "in the framework" matters

The resolver lives at the datasource layer, which means every other in-core feature composes with it by construction. The background job queue, association loading, the DI request-scoped service container — none of them needed extra integration work to be tenant-aware. They share the same datasource resolution.

Compare:

- **Rails:** `apartment` gem ([repo](https://github.com/influitive/apartment)) — community package with a long history of breaking against ORM internals across releases.
- **Laravel:** `stancl/tenancy` ([site](https://tenancyforlaravel.com/)) — middleware and per-request init overhead from a package.
- **Django:** `django-tenants` ([repo](https://github.com/django-tenants/django-tenants)) — schema-only by default.

Each works, none is part of the framework. Wheels 4.0 puts the resolver in core because tenant-awareness is a property of the request, not a feature you opt into.

## Tenant-aware background jobs

This is the part that separates a framework-level solution from a plugin-level one. When a job is enqueued from tenant A's request, the tenant context is persisted with the job. When the worker picks it up — different process, different host, hours later — the framework restores tenant context before `perform()` runs.

```cfm
component extends="wheels.Job" {
    function config() {
        super.config();
        this.queue = "reports";
    }
    public void function perform(struct data = {}) {
        var orders = model("Order").findAll();   // tenant A's orders, automatically
        generateMonthlyReport(orders);
    }
}
```

No "tenant ID as payload field" ceremony. No `with_tenant(tenant) { ... }` wrapper around every `perform` body. No unit test that accidentally passes because it happened to run against the right default datasource. The `model("Order").findAll()` call inside the job behaves exactly the way it would inside the controller that enqueued it.

Pairs naturally with yesterday's post on the [DB-backed job queue](https://blog.wheels.dev/posts/background-jobs-without-redis/).

## When NOT to use framework-level multi-tenancy

Honesty clause. There are places where you *want* to escape the tenant context, and pretending otherwise makes the feature worse, not better.

- **Admin and ops consoles.** The whole point of an internal admin is cross-tenant visibility. "Which tenants signed up this week?" "Which tenants are approaching their rate limit?" Those queries cannot run inside a tenant's datasource. Exit the tenant context explicitly, or wire a dedicated system datasource for admin reads.
- **Cross-tenant reports and billing.** Same rule. Monthly invoicing, aggregate usage metrics, platform-wide analytics — these live in a system-level datasource with deliberate, audited queries. Treat the escape hatch as a deliberate exception, not a framework fight.

The framework makes the right thing easy. It doesn't make the cross-cutting thing impossible. Both matter.

## Migrations and seeding per tenant

Each tenant database gets the same migration set. `wheels dbmigrate latest` targets per-tenant datasources — either one at a time or across all registered tenants in a loop. Seeding respects the active tenant context, so `seeds.cfm` runs against the right database without special casing.

Adding a tenant: create the datasource, run migrations, run seeds. Removing a tenant: destroy the datasource. There is no row-leak risk to audit because there are no rows to leave behind.

## Operational story

Per-datasource backup and restore. Per-datasource scaling. A tenant hammering CPU doesn't starve the others. A tenant requesting GDPR erasure is a `DROP DATABASE` away from complete.

One detail: the rate limiter's database storage lives on the application datasource, not per-tenant. That's deliberate — you want cross-tenant rate-limit visibility for abuse detection, and you don't want to provision that table inside every customer database.

## Links

- [Full audit § Multi-tenancy](https://github.com/wheels-dev/wheels/blob/develop/docs/releases/wheels-4.0-audit.md)
- [PR #1951 — Tenant-aware datasource switching](https://github.com/wheels-dev/wheels/pull/1951)
- [Yesterday's post — DB-backed job queue](https://blog.wheels.dev/posts/background-jobs-without-redis/)
- [Multi-tenancy guide](https://guides.wheels.dev/v4-0-0-snapshot/digging-deeper/multi-tenancy/)
- [Background jobs guide](https://guides.wheels.dev/v4-0-0-snapshot/digging-deeper/background-jobs/)
- [Middleware pipeline](https://guides.wheels.dev/v4-0-0-snapshot/core-concepts/middleware-pipeline/)

## Question for the thread

If you're running production multi-tenant SaaS today, what's your tenant identity source — subdomain, path prefix, header, JWT claim, or something else? And how does it interact with your auth layer? That's the area we expect 4.0.x to want the most polish.

**Read the full post:** https://blog.wheels.dev/posts/multi-tenancy-built-in/

nodes.body:
# GraphQL API Support — API Platform

---

## 1. Overview

GraphQL becomes a new first-class artifact kind alongside `RestApi`, `LlmProvider`, `LlmProxy`, and `Mcp` — onboarded, deployed, and governed through the same control-plane/data-plane pipeline, not bolted on as a generic REST pass-through. 

---

## 2. Goals and Non-Goals (v1)

**Goals:**
- Create, read, update, delete, and deploy a GraphQL API through the same control-plane lifecycle as a REST API.
- Onboard a GraphQL schema either by supplying SDL directly or by pointing at a live endpoint and letting the platform introspect it.
- Proxy GraphQL query/mutation traffic (single `POST` endpoint) through the existing Envoy/policy-engine data plane.
- Reuse every generic QoS policy that applies cleanly (auth, subscription validation, CORS, header mediation, analytics/logging) and add a small number of GraphQL-specific policies for the concerns REST has no equivalent of (query depth/complexity, introspection exposure).

**Non-goals (v1):**
- GraphQL subscriptions / WebSocket proxying — no WebSocket-upgrade handling exists anywhere in the gateway-runtime data plane today (confirmed: no `Upgrade`/websocket filter chain code in `gateway/gateway-controller/pkg/xds/translator.go`); this is real, separately-scoped data-plane work, not a config toggle.
- Persisted queries / automatic persisted queries (APQ) — Phase 2 candidate, not required for a working v1.
- A dedicated GraphQL test console in `api-portal` beyond what already exists (see §9.2) — the existing GraphiQL-style tryout stays as-is.
- Per-field authorization (GraphQL shield-style field-level access control) — out of scope; authZ remains at the API/operation-set level, same granularity as REST today.

---

## 3. Artifact Model

### 3.1 Kind constant

`platform-api/internal/constants/constants.go:76-84` defines the artifact kind discriminator:

```go
const (
    RestApi             = "RestApi"
    WebSubApi           = "WebSubApi"
    WebBrokerApi        = "WebBrokerApi"
    LLMProvider         = "LlmProvider"
    LLMProviderTemplate = "LlmProviderTemplate"
    LLMProxy            = "LlmProxy"
    MCPProxy            = "Mcp"
)
```

Add a new sibling:

```go
GraphQLApi = "GraphQLApi"
```

This is a **different axis** from the existing `APITypeGraphQL = "GRAPHQL"` / `APISubTypeGraphQL = "GQL"` constants at `constants.go:101,111`. Those are dev-portal **content-type** discriminators (`spec.type: GRAPHQL` in an `api-portal` sample, consumed by `apiContentController.js`'s `SPEC_FORMAT_MAP`) — they are declared in platform-api but, per direct grep, never read anywhere in the Go codebase today. Do not conflate the two: `Kind = "GraphQLApi"` is the platform-api/gateway-controller artifact discriminator this spec adds; `APITypeGraphQL = "GRAPHQL"` is the pre-existing (currently dead in Go, live in `api-portal`'s JS) content-type tag. When platform-api starts emitting real GraphQL artifacts, wire `APITypeGraphQL` into whatever payload `api-portal` reads artifact type from, rather than leaving it dead — see §9.2.

**Where the constant actually lands.** `constants.GraphQLApi` is what gets written into the shared `artifacts.type` column, in the exact same place REST writes `constants.RestApi`:

```go
// internal/repository/api.go:73 (REST)
Type: constants.RestApi,

// internal/repository/graphql_api.go:73 (GraphQL)
Type: constants.GraphQLApi,
```

Both are the `Type` field of the `model.Artifact{}` passed to `artifactRepo.Create(tx, ...)` inside each kind's own `CreateAPI`/`Create` method, in the same DB transaction as the kind-specific detail-table insert (`rest_apis`/`graphql_apis`) — this is the header-row write the shared `artifacts` table (§3.3) depends on.

### 3.2 Extension mechanism: core kind, not a plugin

Two precedents exist in this codebase for adding an artifact kind:

| | Core kind (`RestApi`, `LlmProvider`, `LlmProxy`, `Mcp`) | Plugin kind (`WebSubApi`, `WebBrokerApi`) |
|---|---|---|
| Registration | Pre-seeded in `NewArtifactTableRegistry()` (`platform-api/internal/repository/artifact_tables.go:47-71`) | Registered at runtime via `deps.ArtifactTableRegistry.Register(...)` inside a `Plugin.Init()` (`platform-api/plugins/eventgateway/plugin.go:111-114`) |
| Build | Always compiled in | Gated behind a Go build tag (`//go:build experimental`, `eventgateway/plugin.go:1`) |
| Schema DDL | Baked into `platform-api/internal/database/schema.sql` (and `.postgres.sql`/`.sqlserver.sql`) | `//go:embed`-ded by the plugin itself, applied via `db.InitSchemaSQL` only for SQLite at `Init()` time (`plugin.go:63-73,116-126`) |
| Scopes | Declared directly in `platform-api/resources/openapi.yaml` | Declared in the plugin's own embedded OpenAPI fragment, returned via `Plugin.OpenAPISpec()` and merged into the scope registry at startup |

**Decision: ship GraphQL as a core kind**, following the `RestApi`/`LlmProvider`/`LlmProxy`/`Mcp` pattern — pre-seeded in `NewArtifactTableRegistry()`, schema baked directly into `schema.sql` (and the Postgres/SQL Server variants), scopes declared directly in `resources/openapi.yaml`, no build tag. (An earlier draft of this spec recommended the compile-time-plugin approach used by `WebSubApi`/`WebBrokerApi`, for staged/dark rollout; that tradeoff was considered and explicitly declined — GraphQL ships compiled in from day one, matching how REST/LLM/MCP already work, in favor of simplicity over a reversible dark-ship option.) This also removes the asymmetry the plugin approach would have introduced: gateway-controller's `graphql_apis` table (§3.3) is core there too, since gateway-controller has no generalized plugin system as broad as platform-api's `internal/plugin` — with both sides now core, "is GraphQL compiled in" is no longer a question either side needs to ask.

### 3.3 Database schema

**platform-api** (`platform-api/internal/database/schema.sql`) — a new core table, following the `rest_apis` shape at `schema.sql:68-100` exactly, added directly to the core `schema.sql` (and its `.postgres.sql`/`.sqlserver.sql` siblings) per §3.2's core-kind decision, not embedded in a plugin:

```sql
-- graphql_apis table (core schema, same file/dialects as rest_apis)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS graphql_apis (
    uuid VARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,
    organization_uuid VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    handle VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    display_name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    version VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'v1.0',
    project_uuid VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    description VARCHAR(1023),
    lifecycle_status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'CREATED',
    configuration BLOB NOT NULL,       -- JSON: SDL + upstream + policies (§4)
    data_version VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT '1.0',
    origin VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'control_plane',
    created_by VARCHAR(200),
    created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_by VARCHAR(200),
    updated_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    FOREIGN KEY (uuid) REFERENCES artifacts(uuid) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    FOREIGN KEY (organization_uuid) REFERENCES organizations(uuid) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    FOREIGN KEY (project_uuid) REFERENCES projects(uuid) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    UNIQUE(organization_uuid, handle)
);
```

Pre-seeded directly in `NewArtifactTableRegistry()` (`platform-api/internal/repository/artifact_tables.go:47-71`), alongside the other three core entries — not registered at runtime via a plugin's `Init()`:

```go
r.Register(ArtifactTableEntry{
    Table:     "graphql_apis",
    KindAlias: constants.GraphQLApi,
    KindKeys:  []string{"graphql-api", constants.GraphQLApi},
})
```

**gateway-controller** (`gateway/gateway-controller/pkg/storage/gateway-controller-db.sql`) — the existing comment at lines 40-43 already documents this exact extension point:

> *"Note: websub_apis, webbroker_apis, and webhook_secrets tables are NOT defined here. They are event-gateway-specific and owned by the event-gateway-controller module ... which applies its own supplemental DDL against this same database at startup."*

Following that pattern, a `graphql_apis` table is a one-column-identical clone of `rest_apis` (`gateway-controller-db.sql:32-38`):

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS graphql_apis (
    uuid TEXT NOT NULL,
    gateway_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    configuration TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (gateway_id, uuid),
    FOREIGN KEY(gateway_id, uuid) REFERENCES artifacts(gateway_id, uuid) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
```

This was always the natural choice on the gateway-controller side regardless of the platform-api decision in §3.2 — gateway-controller has no existing `Plugin`-style compile-time module system as generalized as `platform-api/internal/plugin` (event-gateway's own controller is a genuinely separate binary/module, `event-gateway/gateway-controller`, with its own `pkg/dbschema`), and GraphQL doesn't need that weight since it's not a separate product. `graphql_apis` is always compiled in, gated only by whether the artifact kind is ever actually synced down (an org with no GraphQL APIs never populates the table).

### 3.4 How the two schemas relate

The two `graphql_apis` tables above look nearly identical but are not the same data, and there is no live foreign key between them — they live in physically separate databases (a central multi-tenant platform-api DB vs. a local per-gateway-instance DB, often even different engines). The relationship is established entirely through the deployment/sync pipeline, keyed on a shared `uuid` value.

| | platform-api | gateway-controller |
|---|---|---|
| Scoping column | `organization_uuid` (multi-tenant, one central DB for every org) | `gateway_id` (one local DB per gateway instance) |
| `artifacts` primary key | `uuid` alone | `(gateway_id, uuid)` — composite |
| Rows per artifact | Exactly one, regardless of how many gateways it's deployed to | One per `(gateway, artifact)` pair — an API deployed to 3 gateways has 3 local rows, one per gateway's own DB |
| Extra bookkeeping columns | none beyond `type` | `desired_state`, `cp_sync_status`, `cp_sync_info`, `cp_artifact_id`, `deployment_id` — GitOps reconciliation state |
| Role | Source of truth — where the API is created/edited | Local cache — what *this specific gateway* currently believes it should be running |

```
platform-api (control plane — one DB, all orgs)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ artifacts (uuid, type='GraphQLApi', org_uuid) │
│ graphql_apis (uuid PK, configuration BLOB)    │  ← authoring config: sdl, upstream, policies
│ deployments (artifact_uuid → gateway_uuid)    │  ← "deploy this API to that gateway"
│ deployment_status (artifact_uuid, gateway_uuid, status)
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                     │
                     │  BuildGraphQLAPIDeploymentYAML(model.API) → deployment YAML,
                     │  pushed/pulled over the control-plane websocket sync (§6.4)
                     ▼
gateway-controller (data plane — one DB PER gateway)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ artifacts (gateway_id=<this gateway>, uuid=   │  ← SAME uuid as the platform-api row
│            <same uuid>, desired_state, ...)   │
│ graphql_apis (gateway_id, uuid, configuration │  ← rendered deployment config, NOT a
│               TEXT)                           │     byte-copy of the authoring blob
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Two consequences worth being explicit about, since both are easy to get wrong when implementing the sync path:

1. **The `configuration` blob is not the same document on both sides.** platform-api's blob is the authoring shape (`CreateGraphQLAPIRequest` — `sdl`, `upstream`, `policies`, `subscriptionPlans`, per §4). gateway-controller's blob is the *deployment YAML* shape produced by `BuildGraphQLAPIDeploymentYAML` (§6.4) — a derived, rendered form. This mirrors how REST APIs already work (`BuildAPIDeploymentYAML` → `dto.APIDeploymentYAML`) and is exactly why §6.4 flags that the historical upstream-auth-dropping bug lives in that transform step, not in either table's schema.
2. **Multiplicity differs by design.** Deploying one GraphQL API to 3 gateways yields 1 platform-api row and 3 independent gateway-controller rows (one per gateway's own local DB). Undeploying from a single gateway only touches that gateway's local row (`desired_state` flips, or the row is removed) — the platform-api row, and the other two gateways' local rows, are untouched.

### 3.5 Audit logging

platform-api keeps a single, kind-agnostic `audit` table — one row per mutation, not per kind:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS audit (
   uuid VARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,
   action VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,           -- "CREATE" / "UPDATE" / "DELETE"
   resource_uuid VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
   resource_type VARCHAR(50),             -- "rest_api", "graphql_api", ...
   organization_uuid VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
   performed_by VARCHAR(200),
   performed_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

The `AuditRepository` interface is a single generic method — `Record(action, resourceUUID, resourceType, orgUUID, performedBy string) error` (`internal/repository/interfaces.go:413-415`) — called fire-and-forget (`_ = ...`, error discarded) so an audit-write failure never fails the underlying API operation. REST's `APIService` calls it at exactly three points, never on read:

```go
_ = s.auditRepo.Record("CREATE", apiUUID, "rest_api", orgUUID, createdBy)   // api.go:178
_ = s.auditRepo.Record("UPDATE", apiUUID, "rest_api", orgUUID, updatedBy)   // api.go:407
_ = s.auditRepo.Record("DELETE", apiUUID, "rest_api", orgUUID, deletedBy)   // api.go:480
```

`GraphQLAPIService` mirrors all three call sites exactly, `resource_type = "graphql_api"` in place of `"rest_api"`:

```go
_ = s.auditRepo.Record("CREATE", m.ID, "graphql_api", orgUUID, createdBy)          // graphql_api.go:219
_ = s.auditRepo.Record("UPDATE", existing.ID, "graphql_api", orgUUID, updatedBy)   // graphql_api.go:452
_ = s.auditRepo.Record("DELETE", existing.ID, "graphql_api", orgUUID, deletedBy)   // graphql_api.go:483
```

One cosmetic difference, not a functional gap: GraphQL's call sites are each wrapped in `if s.auditRepo != nil { ... }`, while REST calls `s.auditRepo.Record(...)` unconditionally. `server.go` always constructs a real `AuditRepository` for both services, so the guard never actually triggers — it's extra defensiveness, not a behavioral divergence. Worth removing only if strict byte-for-byte parity with REST's service file is a goal.

```go
// GraphQLAPI represents a GraphQL API artifact entity.
type GraphQLAPI struct {
    ID              string            `json:"id" db:"uuid"`
    Handle          string            `json:"handle" db:"handle"`
    Name            string            `json:"displayName" db:"display_name"`
    Kind            string            `json:"kind" db:"kind"`
    Description     string            `json:"description,omitempty" db:"description"`
    Version         string            `json:"version" db:"version"`
    CreatedBy       string            `json:"createdBy,omitempty" db:"created_by"`
    UpdatedBy       string            `json:"updatedBy,omitempty" db:"updated_by"`
    ProjectID       string            `json:"projectId" db:"project_uuid"`
    OrganizationID  string            `json:"organizationId" db:"organization_uuid"`

    UpdatedAt       time.Time         `json:"updatedAt,omitempty" db:"updated_at"`
    LifeCycleStatus string            `json:"lifeCycleStatus,omitempty" db:"lifecycle_status"`
    Configuration   GraphQLAPIConfig  `json:"configuration" db:"-"`
    Origin          string            `json:"origin,omitempty" db:"origin"`
    DataVersion     string            `json:"dataVersion,omitempty" db:"data_version"`
}

type GraphQLAPIConfig struct {
    Name              string          `json:"name,omitempty"`
    Version           string          `json:"version,omitempty"`
    Context           *string         `json:"context,omitempty"`   // e.g. "/countries/$version" — same $version substitution as REST
    SDL               string          `json:"sdl"`                 // the GraphQL schema, always stored resolved (never a document-supplied schemaLocation — xxe-xml-processing.md §3 applies by analogy)
    IntrospectionMode string          `json:"introspectionMode,omitempty"` // "SDL" | "ENDPOINT" — how the schema was obtained; see §5
    Upstream          UpstreamConfig  `json:"upstream,omitempty"`  // reused as-is from model/upstream.go — single endpoint, no per-operation paths
    Policies          []Policy        `json:"policies,omitempty"`  // reused as-is from model/api.go
    SubscriptionPlans []string        `json:"subscriptionPlans,omitempty"`
}
```

**Deliberately absent compared to `RestAPIConfig`:** `Transport []string` and `Operations []Operation`. GraphQL has no per-resource/per-verb operation list — there is exactly one logical endpoint per API, matching the single-route design in §6. `Channels` (WebSub-only) is likewise absent.

## 5. Onboarding — Two Paths

Both converge on the same `GraphQLAPIConfig.SDL` field.

### 5.1 Direct SDL import

The publisher supplies the SDL directly, via any of three input mechanisms — all converge on the same `CreateGraphQLAPIRequest.sdl` field server-side:

1. **Inline (`application/json`, `sdl` field)** — the SDL text pasted directly into the JSON create/update body. The original, simplest path.
2. **File upload (`multipart/form-data`)** — the same endpoint additionally accepts a `GraphQLAPIMultipartRequest` body: a `metadata` field (the same JSON body as path 1, JSON-encoded as a string, with `sdl`/`sdlUrl` ignored if present) plus an `sdlFile` file part. The uploaded content always wins over anything in `metadata`. Parsed via `internal/utils/graphql_multipart.go`'s `ParseGraphQLAPIMultipartRequest` — read entirely in memory through a size-limited reader (5 MiB), never written to a temp file (`file-access.md` directive 3).
3. **By URL (`sdlUrl` field, either content type)** — a URL to a raw SDL document (e.g. a `raw.githubusercontent.com` link), fetched server-side and used as `sdl`. Distinct from §5.2's `upstream.main.url`: this is a plain HTTP(S) GET of a static file, not a live introspection query, and is fetched through `utils.FetchOpenAPISpecFromURL` — the same public-internet-only SSRF-hardened helper LLM Provider Templates already use for `metadata.openapiSpecUrl` (`ssrf-prevention.md` directive 6: one shared helper, not a new one-off client). Loopback/private/link-local/metadata addresses are refused, same as any other public-vendor-doc fetch; this path is not meant for a tenant's own in-cluster backend (`upstream.main.url` is, and uses the more permissive `NewUpstreamFetchClient` policy instead — see §5.2). `sdl` and `sdlUrl` are mutually exclusive on a single request (`ValidationFailed` if both are set); the byte ceiling reuses `cfg.Server.OpenAPISpecMaxFetchBytes` rather than a new GraphQL-only config key, since it's the same class of bounded external-document fetch.

All three produce `introspectionMode = "SDL"` on the stored record — the distinction between "pasted," "uploaded," and "fetched by URL" is not retained after creation, only "was this schema supplied directly vs. derived via live introspection" (§5.2).

**There was no existing OpenAPI-equivalent ingestion pipeline to reuse for parsing/validating the schema itself.** Investigation of the REST API creation path found there is **no third-party OpenAPI parser/validator** anywhere in this repo (no `kin-openapi`, no schema library in `go.work.sum`) — REST APIs are defined natively via `operations[]`/`policies[]` JSON, not by uploading and parsing an OpenAPI document; there is no file-upload or URL-fetch mechanism for REST API definitions at the platform-api level at all. `platform-api/internal/dto/openapi_spec.go` is output-only (exports an OpenAPI doc from an already-stored REST API; never ingests one). This means the GraphQL SDL parser (`github.com/vektah/gqlparser/v2`, Apache-2.0) was a genuinely new class of dependency on the platform-api side — there was nothing to copy from REST's ingestion path because REST doesn't have one; only the generic file/URL *transport* mechanisms (multipart parsing, SSRF-hardened fetch) had precedent to reuse.

### 5.2 Create from endpoint via introspection

The publisher supplies only `upstream.main.url`; platform-api runs the standard GraphQL introspection query (`{ __schema { ... } }`) against that endpoint at creation time and derives the SDL server-side. This is the primary flow in Bijira's own GraphQL implementation (`EndpointSource.tsx` in `wso2-enterprise/apim-saas` PR #1602) and is the more natural GraphQL-native UX, since virtually every GraphQL server exposes introspection by default.

**This is an outbound request to a user-supplied URL and must go through the exact same SSRF-hardened path REST/LLM/MCP upstream validation already uses** — `ssrf-prevention.md` directive 6 is explicit that every upstream validator must call one shared helper, not reimplement a thinner check. Grep `gateway-controller/pkg/config/api_validator.go`, `mcp_validator.go`, `llm_validator.go` for the existing `validateUpstream*` naming convention and add `validateGraphQLUpstream` (or reuse the REST validator directly, since the shape — a single URL, no per-resource paths — is actually simpler than REST's) calling the same shared `netguard`-style helper. Do not write a new one-off HTTP client for the introspection call.

The resolved SDL is stored identically regardless of which path produced it — `IntrospectionMode` is metadata only (drives whether the Console re-offers "re-introspect" vs. "re-upload" on edit), not a different storage shape.

### 5.3 What's explicitly not resolved server-side

Per `xxe-xml-processing.md`/`js-ssrf-prevention.md`'s shared principle (never auto-dereference a document-supplied secondary location): if the introspected schema or an uploaded SDL contains directives pointing at further remote schemas (federation `@link`, custom directives with URLs), those are **not** auto-fetched. Federation is out of scope for v1 (§2).

## 6. Gateway Controller Integration

### 6.1 Why REST's per-operation routing doesn't apply

`gateway/gateway-controller/pkg/transform/restapi.go:82-106` (`RestAPITransformer.Transform`) builds one `models.Route` per `apiData.Operations[]` entry, keyed by method+path, because REST exposes N resources over N method/path combinations. GraphQL exposes exactly one logical endpoint (conventionally `POST <context>`) — the "operation" (query/mutation name) is identified by the request body, not the URL. Building N=1 route is correct; trying to force GraphQL into the per-operation loop would be actively wrong, not just unnecessary.

### 6.2 Extension point: `ConfigTransformer`, not the legacy per-Kind `if`

`gateway/gateway-controller/pkg/xds/translator.go:722-751` tries a kind-keyed transformer map first, and only falls back to hardcoded per-`Kind` `if`/`switch` logic (the `WebSubApi` special case, and `translateAPIConfig` for everything else) when no transformer is registered for that kind:

```go
if transformer, ok := t.transformers[cfg.Kind]; ok {
    rdc, transformErr := transformer.Transform(cfg)
    // ... routesList, clusterList, err = t.translateRuntimeConfig(rdc)
}
```

`models.ConfigTransformer` (`pkg/models/runtime_deploy_config.go:140-142`) is a one-method interface:

```go
type ConfigTransformer interface {
    Transform(cfg *StoredConfig) (*RuntimeDeployConfig, error)
}
```

**GraphQL should implement this interface directly** (`transform.NewGraphQLAPITransformer`, mirroring `NewRestAPITransformer` at `restapi.go:48-60`) and get wired into the *existing* generic `translateRuntimeConfig` pipeline — no changes needed to `translator.go`'s core translation logic, Envoy route/cluster building, or the policy-engine's xDS resource generation, all of which already consume the kind-agnostic `RuntimeDeployConfig` shape (`runtime_deploy_config.go:27-38`).

A GraphQL `Transform()` produces exactly one `Route`:

```go
rdc.Routes["graphql"] = &models.Route{
    Method:        "POST",
    Path:          apiData.Context,   // e.g. "/countries/v1" — no operation-path suffix
    PathMatchType: "Exact",
    Upstream:      models.RouteUpstream{ClusterKey: "main", Default: &policyenginev1.UpstreamInfo{ /* ... */ }},
}
```

`PolicyChainResolver: "route-key"` (the same value `RestAPITransformer` sets at `restapi.go:101`) is correct here too — with exactly one route, "resolve the policy chain by the matched Envoy route" needs no GraphQL-specific resolver.

**Operation-level (per-query/per-mutation) policies do not need a new resolver.** MCP already solved the identical problem — one route serving many logical operations (tools) — and it's worth being precise about how, since an earlier draft of this section claimed MCP has a working `"mcp-tool"` resolver for this; it doesn't. `"mcp-tool"` exists only as a code comment (`runtime_deploy_config.go:33`, `resolver.go:26`) — it was never registered, and the policy-engine's resolver registry contains only `"route-key"` (`resolver.go`'s `init()`). MCP is transformed by the same `RestAPITransformer` as REST and gets the same single `"route-key"`-resolved chain for its one route.

### 6.3 Wiring — three places to touch, not one

Adding the transformer to `pkg/transform/registry.go` alone is not sufficient; three registration points exist and all three currently hardcode the four known kinds:

1. **`gateway/gateway-controller/pkg/transform/registry.go:39-47`** — `Registry.Transform`'s `switch cfg.Kind` needs a `case "GraphQLApi":` arm. This function backs *both* the Envoy xDS path (via `translator.SetTransformers`) and the policy-engine xDS path (via `policyManager.SetTransformers`, `policyxds/manager.go:51-52`) — miss this and GraphQL policy chains silently never resolve even if Envoy routing works.
2. **`gateway/gateway-controller/cmd/controller/main.go:444-449`** — the `translator.SetTransformers(map[string]models.ConfigTransformer{...})` call needs a `"GraphQLApi": transformerRegistry` entry alongside the existing four.
3. **`gateway/gateway-controller/api/management-openapi.yaml`** — add a `/graphql-apis` path group, following the exact shape of the existing `/rest-apis` group (`/rest-apis:19`, `/rest-apis/{id}:124`, `.../api-keys:261`, `.../api-keys/{apiKeyName}/regenerate:349`, `.../api-keys/{apiKeyName}:409`; `RestAPI` schema at `components.schemas:2843`; tags block at `5092`).

### 6.4 Deployment YAML

`BuildAPIDeploymentYAML` (`platform-api/internal/utils/api.go:471-553`) renders `model.API` into the YAML manifest pushed to the gateway; a `BuildGraphQLAPIDeploymentYAML` follows the identical shape, substituting `RestAPIConfig` for `GraphQLAPIConfig` and omitting the `Operations`/`Channels` blocks entirely (§4). Note the historical bug this file had for REST — `dto.UpstreamTarget` at `platform-api/internal/dto/api.go:157-161` currently carries only `URL`/`Ref`, no `Auth` field, so `BuildAPIDeploymentYAML` drops `upstream.main.auth`/`upstream.sandbox.auth` before the YAML ever reaches the gateway (confirmed still present in this checkout, not yet fixed). **Do not copy this gap into the GraphQL deployment builder** — give `GraphQLUpstreamTarget` (or whatever the shared/renamed type ends up being) an `Auth *model.UpstreamAuth` field from day one, matching what MCP Proxy's `BuildMCPDeploymentYAML` already does correctly.

#### 6.4.1 Standalone gateway artifact YAML

The same `GraphQLApi` shape is also applied directly to a standalone gateway, with no control plane involved, via `ap gateway apply --file <file>.yaml` (`cli/src/cmd/gateway/apply.go`) — this is the format users hand-author, distinct from the CP-generated deployment YAML in §6.4.

```yaml

kind: GraphQLApi
metadata:
  name: countries-graphql-v1
spec:
  displayName: Countries
  version: v1
  context: /countries/$version
  upstream:
    main:
      url: http://countries-service:4000/graphql
  policies:
    - name: jwt-auth
      version: v1
```

`sdl` is not required at the gateway-controller (GraphQL routing never consumes the schema).

```yaml
        omit it and provide a reachable `upstream.main.url` exposing GraphQL
        introspection — the schema is derived server-side in the latter case (§5.2).
        The API is associated with a project, which must belong to the organization
        specified in the JWT token.
      operationId: CreateGraphQLAPI
      security:
        - OAuth2Security:
            - ap:graphql_api:create
            - ap:graphql_api:manage
      tags:
        - GraphQL APIs
      requestBody:
        description: GraphQL API object that needs to be added
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/CreateGraphQLAPIRequest'
        required: true
      responses:
        '201':
          description: GraphQL API created successfully
          headers:
            Location:
              $ref: '#/components/headers/Location'
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/GraphQLAPI'
        '400':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/BadRequest'
        '401':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Unauthorized'
        '403':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Forbidden'
        '404':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/NotFound'
        '409':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Conflict'
        '422':
          description: The provided endpoint could not be used to derive a GraphQL schema (introspection failed or was rejected), or the supplied SDL failed to parse.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/ErrorResponse'
        '500':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/InternalServerError'

  /graphql-apis/{graphqlApiId}:
    get:
      summary: Get GraphQL API by ID
      operationId: GetGraphQLAPI
      security:
        - OAuth2Security:
            - ap:graphql_api:read
            - ap:graphql_api:manage
      tags:
        - GraphQL APIs
      parameters:
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/apiId'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: GraphQL API retrieved successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/GraphQLAPI'
        '400':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/BadRequest'
        '401':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Unauthorized'
        '404':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/NotFound'
        '500':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/InternalServerError'
    put:
      summary: Update GraphQL API
      description: |
        Updates an existing GraphQL API's details, including re-supplying `sdl` or
        re-introspecting `upstream.main.url` to pick up a changed backend schema.
      operationId: UpdateGraphQLAPI
      security:
        - OAuth2Security:
            - ap:graphql_api:update
            - ap:graphql_api:manage
      tags:
        - GraphQL APIs
      parameters:
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/apiId'
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/GraphQLAPI'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: GraphQL API updated successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/GraphQLAPI'
        '400':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/BadRequest'
        '401':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Unauthorized'
        '403':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Forbidden'
        '404':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/NotFound'
        '409':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Conflict'
        '422':
          description: Re-introspection or re-parsing of the updated schema failed.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/ErrorResponse'
        '500':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/InternalServerError'
    delete:
      summary: Delete GraphQL API
      operationId: DeleteGraphQLAPI
      security:
        - OAuth2Security:
            - ap:graphql_api:delete
            - ap:graphql_api:manage
      tags:
        - GraphQL APIs
      parameters:
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/apiId'
      responses:
        '204':
          description: GraphQL API deleted successfully
        '400':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/BadRequest'
        '401':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Unauthorized'
        '403':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/Forbidden'
        '404':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/NotFound'
        '500':
          $ref: '#/components/responses/InternalServerError'
```

`/graphql-apis/{graphqlApiId}/gateways`, `.../api-keys[/{apiKeyId}]`, and `.../deployments[/{deploymentId}[/undeploy|/restore]]` are added identically to their `/rest-apis/...` counterparts (`platform-api/resources/openapi.yaml:522,604,653,747,834,898,957`) — same parameters, same response shapes, same scope-suffix convention (`ap:graphql_api:gateway:*`, `ap:graphql_api:api_key:*`, `ap:graphql_api:deployment:*`, per §8). They're pure path/schema-name substitutions with no GraphQL-specific behavior, so they're not re-drafted in full here.

Also add `GraphQL APIs` to the `tags:` block (mirroring `REST APIs` at `openapi.yaml:9003`) and `ap:graphql_api:*` entries to the `OAuth2Security.scopes` map and its description block (`openapi.yaml:4732` and `4832-4833`) — directly in this core file, per §3.2's core-kind decision.

**Codegen, not hand-written structs.** Both `platform-api/api/generated.go` and `gateway/gateway-controller/pkg/api/management/generated.go` are `oapi-codegen`-generated (`DO NOT EDIT` header in both). Edit the YAML in both specs, then run `make generate` (platform-api — see `platform-api/Makefile:114-121`; this also runs the `yq` pass that injects `x-oapi-codegen-extra-tags.binding=required` from each schema's `required` list before invoking `oapi-codegen`) and the equivalent gateway-controller generate target. Docs under `docs/rest-apis/platform-api/` are generated separately via `make generate-apidocs` (`platform-api/Makefile:123-129`, `widdershins` + `split-openapi.sh`) — re-run after any path/schema change so the published reference stays in sync.

### 6.6 Example Requests and Responses

**Create — via direct SDL:**

```http
POST /api/v0.9/graphql-apis
Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "displayName": "Countries GraphQL API",
  "description": "Public GraphQL API for querying country/region reference data",
  "context": "/countries",
  "version": "v1.0",
  "projectId": "default-project",
  "sdl": "type Query {\n  countries: [Country]\n  country(code: ID!): Country\n}\ntype Country {\n  code: String\n  name: String\n  capital: String\n}",
  "upstream": {
    "main": { "url": "https://countries.trevorblades.com/graphql" }
  },
  "policies": [
    { "name": "jwt-auth", "version": "1.0.0" }
  ],
  "subscriptionPlans": ["Gold", "Silver"]
}
```

**Response — 201 Created**

```json
{
  "id": "countries-graphql-api",
  "displayName": "Countries GraphQL API",
  "description": "Public GraphQL API for querying country/region reference data",
  "context": "/countries",
  "version": "v1.0",
  "projectId": "default-project",
  "sdl": "type Query {\n  countries: [Country]\n  country(code: ID!): Country\n}\ntype Country {\n  code: String\n  name: String\n  capital: String\n}",
  "introspectionMode": "SDL",
  "upstream": {
    "main": { "url": "https://countries.trevorblades.com/graphql" }
  },
  "policies": [
    { "name": "jwt-auth", "version": "1.0.0" }
  ],
  "subscriptionPlans": ["Gold", "Silver"],
  "lifeCycleStatus": "CREATED",
  "kind": "GraphQLApi",
  "readOnly": false,
  "createdAt": "2026-08-11T10:00:00Z",
  "updatedAt": "2026-08-11T10:00:00Z"
}
```

**Create — via endpoint introspection (no `sdl` supplied):**

```http

Content-Type: application/json

    "main": { "url": "https://countries.trevorblades.com/graphql" }

}
```

**Response — 201 Created** *(`sdl` is now server-derived; `introspectionMode` reflects that)*

```json
  "displayName": "Countries GraphQL API",
  "context": "/countries",

  "sdl": "type Query {\n  countries: [Country]\n  country(code: ID!): Country\n}\ntype Country {\n  code: String\n  name: String\n  capital: String\n}",
  "introspectionMode": "ENDPOINT",
```


**Response — 422 Unprocessable Entity** *(generic — never echoes the resolved IP or the specific SSRF/introspection-disabled reason, per `error-handling.md`/`ssrf-prevention.md`)*

**List:**

**Update** — `PUT /api/v0.9/graphql-apis/countries-graphql-api` with a full `GraphQLAPI` body (same shape as create); response `200` with the updated object, same shape as create's `201`.

**Delete:**
