--- ### 🔗 Directus Hub MVP * [Directus Hub MVP – PRD](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012170) * [Repository Structure – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012171) * [Metadata Layer – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012179) * [Jobs Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012180) * [Provider Management Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012181) * [Docker Provider Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012182) * [NPM Provider Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012184) * [Git Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012186) * [Schema-Sync Extension Integration – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012188) * [Backup-Sync Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012191) * [Secrets Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012193) * [Hub Connector Extension – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012195) * [Metrics Layer – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012196) * [Directus Platform Integration – Directus Hub (MVP)](https://github.com/directus/directus/discussions/25544#discussioncomment-14012616) --- ## 1. Overview Directus Hub is a proposed orchestration and control layer for managing multiple Directus Studios. It enables teams to deploy, monitor, back up, and manage the lifecycle of Directus instances at scale. Designed for digital agencies, SaaS teams, and enterprise environments, the Hub introduces an infrastructure-agnostic way to bring consistency and control to multi-studio deployments.
*Figure 1.1 - Directus Hub Overview* The Hub centrally manages multiple Studios, each with its own environments.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 2. Problem Statement As organizations adopt Directus for multiple projects (client-a, client-b, project-a, project-b) or environments (dev, staging, production), the lack of centralized orchestration introduces risk and inefficiency. Current methods rely on CLI tooling, external automation, or manual interventions. Directus Hub addresses this by centralizing studio metadata, automating schema and backup workflows, and integrating with DevOps pipelines.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 3. Goals The Directus Hub is designed to solve operational inefficiencies while also unlocking strategic growth opportunities. Its goals are: - **Centralize management** of multiple Directus Studios across environments and clients. - Standardize schema, access, and extension deployment using **modular definitions**. - Enable **configuration-as-code** for reproducible, version-controlled environments. - Support both **automated and manual execution** via agents, webhooks, CLI, or UI. - **Provide lifecycle orchestration** for provisioning, backups, restores, and cloning. - Offer **observability and governance** features including logs, audit trails, and schema drift detection. - **Improve onboarding and adoption** by enabling template-based studio launches. - Unlock **new monetization paths** and operational features for Directus Pro Cloud.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 4. Target Users & Use Cases **Solo Developer** - Builds apps using Directus Cloud with minimal infrastructure setup. - Needs: A simple way to create and manage staging environments, test schema or extension changes, and deploy updates without DevOps complexity. - Use Case: "I want to spin up a staging studio to try out a new flow and preview content changes—then push those updates to production when I’m ready." **Platform Engineer** - Manages infrastructure, CI/CD, and system configuration. - Needs: Git integration, config-as-code, rollback support. - Use Case: "I want to manage Studio provisioning through versioned templates and GitHub Actions." **Content Admin / Project Manager** - Oversees content structure, user access, environment readiness. - Needs: Easy provisioning, schema previews, job status visibility. - Use Case: "I want to provision a new Studio with our CRM schema and pre-set team roles." **DevOps Engineer** - Automates pipelines, ensures deployment reliability. - Needs: API endpoints, job logs, alerting, environment cloning. - Use Case: "I want failure alerts when backup jobs fail so I can intervene quickly." **Agency Developer / Freelancer** - Builds client-specific Directus instances efficiently. - Needs: One-click provisioning, reusable modules, isolated environments. - Use Case: "I want to clone a preconfigured 'eCommerce Studio' for clients in minutes."

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 5. Landscape and Precedents Directus Hub isn’t the first system to tackle environment orchestration—but it fills a unique gap in the headless CMS ecosystem by offering a dedicated control layer for managing multiple Directus Studios. ### 5.1 Precedents - **Aegir (Drupal):** Aegir directly inspired the vision for Directus Hub. It was an early open-source system for managing multiple Drupal sites with shared templates, backups, and upgrades—all from a central dashboard. While designed for a monolithic CMS, it proved that centralized orchestration of structured content environments is both possible and powerful. - **WHM / cPanel**: WHM offers a centralized interface for provisioning and managing multiple cPanel instances, each representing a separate hosted website. Its model of isolated tenant environments on shared infrastructure—with templated setups, automated backups, and role-based access—closely mirrors the goals of Directus Hub. Though designed for web hosting, WHM and cPanel pioneered accessible multi-instance orchestration long before it became common in modern developer tooling. - **Backstage:** A modern developer portal and service catalog. Its pluggable architecture parallels how Directus Hub models environments, modules, and jobs—and could even be used alongside it. - **Docker Hub:** Introduced the concept of reusable, versioned system artifacts. Directus Hub applies this same pattern to schema modules, templates, and instance blueprints. - **Platform Starter Kits (Vercel, Netlify, etc.):** These tools made one-click deployment mainstream. Directus Hub brings that experience to backend content platforms—with full schema and access control baked in. ### 5.2 Related Infrastructure (Complementary, Not Competitive) Directus Hub integrates with tools teams already use: - **GitHub Actions, AWS Lambda:** Event-based automation and CI/CD. - **Railway, Render, Vercel:** API-driven app hosting and provisioning. - **Docker & Docker Compose:** Declarative local or remote orchestration. - **Terraform, Kubernetes:** Infrastructure-as-code and container orchestration for cloud-native workflows. Directus Hub defines orchestration logic and delegates execution to external systems—whether serverless, containerized, or pipeline-based—based on each team’s preferred stack. ### 5.3 Positioning Unlike general-purpose orchestration platforms, Directus Hub is purpose-built for content teams. It provides schema-aware tooling, backups, and environment visibility—without requiring custom plugins or deep DevOps expertise. It’s turnkey orchestration for the structured content layer.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 6. Core Features - **Studio Provisioning** Create a declarative Studio Definition that outlines a Directus instance’s configuration. This definition can later be used to trigger infrastructure jobs such as provisioning, rebuilds, or teardown. - **Tenant Management** Create, track, and manage tenants across different studios and infrastructure setups. Supports provisioning, data seeding, and lifecycle control for each tenant. - **Environment Management** Track environments like dev, staging, and production per studio. Environments may have different provisioning strategies, access controls, and schema versions. - **Provider Abstraction** Each environment is assigned a provider key—such as `railway`, `vercel`, `aws`, or `manual`—which defines how infrastructure jobs are fulfilled, allowing Directus Hub to support a variety of deployment strategies through a consistent orchestration model. - **Schema Management** Assign reusable schema modules to each studio. Capture, version, and apply schema snapshots. Detect and manage conflicts across assigned modules. - **Access Role Management** Define and assign reusable access control modules—including roles, permissions, and rules—to each studio. These modules are validated against assigned schemas to prevent broken references and maintain security. The system offers visibility into current role configurations and can optionally flag potential risks using logic or AI. - **Data Seeding** Inject predefined data into new or existing studios during provisioning. Useful for populating content models, roles, permissions, or any baseline data needed to make a project usable out of the box. - **Studio Extensions** Assign and manage custom and marketplace extensions on a per-studio and per-environment basis. Each extension is version-controlled and can be tailored to dev, staging, or production environments independently. Extensions are assigned alongside schema and access modules during provisioning or updates, with visibility into what’s installed, where, and at what version. Compatibility is validated to prevent conflicts with schema or core system functionality. - **Flow Management** Manage and version Directus Flows assigned to each studio and environment. Flows can be bundled into reusable modules and deployed alongside schema, access, and extension definitions. The system tracks flow versions and their relationships to other modules, ensuring each environment runs the correct automation logic without conflicts. - **Config-as-Code Support** Studio Definitions, schema modules, and job templates can be stored and versioned in external repositories (e.g., GitHub). This enables reproducibility, auditability, and integration with modern DevOps workflows and CI/CD pipelines. - **Job Orchestration** Trigger and monitor jobs like `provision`, `backup`, `restore`, `rebuild`, and `clone`. Jobs are fulfilled by agents, webhooks, or external systems. A flexible execution model supports both automation and manual handling. - **Manual + Automated Execution** Jobs can be fulfilled via scheduled runners, on-demand execution, external systems (e.g., GitHub Actions), or manually by an admin. This keeps the system flexible and secure. - **Studio Cloning** Duplicate the configuration of an existing studio—including environment variables, schema assignments, and optionally data—to quickly spin up dev/staging copies. - **Backup / Recovery** Generate timestamped database and file backups for any studio/environment. Restore operations can rehydrate instances on demand, with full audit logs. - **Logging & Monitoring** Maintain logs of all job executions, instance status changes, schema deployments, and backups. Use this for audits, debugging, and governance. - **Frontend Provisioning (Planned Optional Feature)** Provision frontend environments alongside backends by integrating with services like Vercel or Railway. Enables full-stack template launches, automated variable injection, and real-time preview deployments.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 7. System Architecture Directus Hub acts as a centralized control plane, purpose-built to manage a distributed network of Directus Studios. It runs as a standalone Directus instance with custom schema and extensions. The system is modular, infrastructure-agnostic, and designed to integrate with various provisioning tools and DevOps pipelines. Rather than executing infrastructure tasks directly, the Hub defines what should happen, tracks state, and delegates fulfillment to external systems like GitHub Actions, Railway, or custom runners. ### 7.1 Core Architectural Layers - **Metadata Layer** Stores persistent data about studios, modules, environments, snapshots, jobs, backups, and system events. This is the single source of truth for orchestration metadata. - **Integration Layer** Connects to external Git repositories for managing studio definitions, modules, and job templates as code. Enables version-controlled, reproducible environments. - **Module Registry** Houses reusable components that can be versioned and assigned to studios: - **Schema Modules**: Define collections, fields, and relationships. - **Access Modules**: Define roles, permissions, and access scopes. - **Extension Modules**: Load extensions into studios with specific versions and build flags. - **Data Seed Modules**: Prepopulate studios with content, roles, or test data. - **Job Engine** Queues and tracks orchestration jobs such as `provision`, `clone`, `backup`, and `restore`. Stores payloads, logs, and fulfillment results. Jobs are designed to be infrastructure-agnostic and can be fulfilled through various execution models. - **Execution Layer** Supports a decoupled execution model driven by the provider assigned to each environment. The provider determines how jobs are fulfilled—whether by API, agent, CI pipeline, or manual input—allowing the Hub to adapt to different infrastructure strategies without changing core logic. - **Internal Agent** – Polling or scheduled task runner - **Webhook Runner** – Webhooks for external services or servers - **CI/CD Integration** – Systems like GitHub Actions, Railway - **Manual Execution** – Admin fulfills jobs via UI and logs results ### 7.2 Operational Lifecycle The Hub coordinates orchestration through a predictable and transparent workflow: 1. **Define** Admins create a new Studio Definition via the UI or CLI (`directus hub create-studio`). They assign schema, access, and seed modules as part of the setup. 2. **Plan** A user initiates an action (manually or via webhook/CI). This queues a job (e.g., `provision`, `rebuild`, `backup`) that includes all required metadata and context. 3. **Execute** The job is picked up by an executor (agent, webhook, CI runner). It performs the task and returns status, logs, and artifacts (e.g., backups or deployment URLs). 4. **Observe** The Hub logs all activity. Admins can track job status, view logs, inspect schema versions, monitor backups, and check studio health—all from a single dashboard. ### 7.3 Studio Provisioning & Control Flow When the Hub provisions a Studio, it assembles a complete configuration from modular inputs—such as schema, flows, roles, extensions, and seed data—based on the selected environment (e.g. Dev, Stage, Prod). This combination is saved as a **Studio Definition**, which becomes the control point for all automation, monitoring, and management tasks tied to that Studio.
*Figure 7.1: Studio Instance Provisioning & Control Flow* This diagram shows how the Hub builds a Studio Definition from modular components. Once defined, the Studio can be deployed and managed consistently using the assigned infrastructure provider or job runner.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 8. Hub Data Model & Collections ### **8.1 Core Collections:** - `studios` - Top-level project containers - `environments` - Studio instances (dev/staging/prod) - `tenants` - Tenants are used to separate data at row or database level under the same studio. (row or database methods) - `providers` – Linked to environments; defines how infrastructure jobs are fulfilled (e.g., Railway, GitHub, AWS) - `schema_modules` - Reusable schema definitions - `access_modules` - Role and permission templates - `extension_modules` - Extensions and extension settings templates - `flow_modules` - Reusable automation logic - `jobs` - Orchestration tasks (provision, backup, restore) - `backups` - Database and file snapshots ### **8.2 Key Relationships:** - Studios → Environments (1:many) - Environments → Modules (many:many via junction tables) - Jobs → Environments (many:1) - Backups → Environments (many:1) ### **8.3 Example Studio Definition:** ```json { "studio_id": "rabbitworks_cms", "provider": "github_actions", "schema_modules": ["blog", "auth"], "access_modules": ["editor_team"], "extensions": ["seo", "custom_extension"], "tenants": [ { "tenant_id": "tenant_42", "database": "rabbitworks_tenant_42", "data_seed": ["demo_users", "default_pages"] }, { "tenant_id": "tenant_43", "database": "rabbitworks_tenant_43", "data_seed": ["minimal_seed"] } ], "environments": { "production": { "url": "https://cms.rabbitworks.com", "metrics_enabled": true, "backup_enabled": true }, "staging": { "url": "https://staging.cms.rabbitworks.com", "metrics_enabled": false, "backup_enabled": false } } }

⬆ Back to top

``` --- ## 9. Tenancy Models Supported by the Directus Hub (Multi-Tenant) The Directus Hub supports three core tenancy models, each with different trade-offs in isolation, portability, and operational complexity. While the Hub manages provisioning, data seeding, destruction, and tenant tracking, some behaviors—such as permission enforcement or multi-database routing—depend on features provided by Directus itself and may vary by implementation. ### 9.1 Shared Studio, Shared Database (Row-Level Permissions) All tenants share the same Directus Studio and the same database. Data is scoped using a `tenant_id` field, with access control enforced via Directus role-based permissions. - **Requires:** Directus support for row-level permissions - **Hub Role:** - Tracks tenants as metadata - Seeds default content tagged with the tenant’s ID - Supports tenant creation and deletion via filtering workflows (complex) - **Isolation:** Low - **Portability:** Low (difficult to extract a single tenant cleanly) - **Best For:** MVPs, internal tools, lightweight SaaS - **Limitations:** - All tenants share schema, logic, and infrastructure - Misconfigured permissions may expose data - Studio failure impacts all tenants - **Resource Usage:** Low at idle; increases with tenant activity ### 9.2 Shared Studio, Separate Databases Tenants share the same Studio instance but have separate databases. The Studio must support routing requests to the correct database based on context (e.g. JWT claims, subdomain, or session). - **Requires:** Directus support for multiple databases per Studio - **Hub Role:** - Clones schema and seeds a new tenant database - Assigns the database to an existing Studio (typically on the same DB server) - Simplifies tenant deployment and teardown - Enables usage-based billing (per DB, access request, or tenant) - Supports clean backups, migrations, and isolated service tiers - **Isolation:** Medium–High - **Portability:** High (each DB can be independently moved or archived) - **Best For:** SaaS with isolated data and shared business logic - **Limitations:** - Depends on future support in Directus core for multi-DB routing - Difficult to run cross-tenant analytics - Studio failure still affects all tenants - **Resource Usage:** Low to moderate; scales with the number of active databases ### 9.3 One Studio per Tenant (Full Isolation) Each tenant has a dedicated Directus Studio instance, deployed independently. Each Studio connects to its own database, which may be on a **shared database server** or its own **fully isolated host**, depending on operational requirements. - **Requires:** Nothing—fully supported by Directus and the Hub - **Hub Role:** - Deploys a new Studio per tenant (via Railway, GitHub Actions, etc.) - Provisions a dedicated database (on shared or separate DB servers) - Applies schema, flows, roles, and seed data from a versioned template - Manages upgrades, tracking, and full tenant lifecycle - **Isolation:** Very High (complete separation at Studio and DB level) - **Portability:** Very High (tenants can be migrated, paused, or archived independently) - **Best For:** Agencies, enterprise clients, white-label platforms, or regulated industries - **Limitations:** - Cross-tenant analytics not feasible without external tooling - **Resource Usage:** High—each tenant consumes independent infrastructure ### 9.4 Consistent Benefits Across All Models Regardless of the tenancy model chosen, the Directus Hub provides the same core value: a centralized control layer for managing studios and tenants at scale. It standardizes provisioning, data seeding, upgrades, and lifecycle tracking across all configurations—whether you're using a single Studio or many, one database or multiple, one database server or several. This enables teams to expand across organizations and environments while maintaining structure and control.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 10. CLI and Deployment Flow The Directus Hub CLI manages the full lifecycle of a studio and its environments—from setup to schema assignments, provisioning, and backup. Each command logs metadata to the Hub and triggers jobs that are fulfilled by agents, webhooks, or external systems. ### 10.1 Key Commands ### `directus hub init` `directus hub init --with-modules --link-git ""` - Initializes a new Hub instance and optional config repo link. - Sets up base collections (`studios`, `jobs`, etc.), permissions, and optional module seeds. ### `studio:create` `directus hub studio:create --name "RabbitWorks CMS"` - Defines a top-level project container. - Adds a new studio and optionally preps default environments. ### `env:provision` `directus hub env:provision --studio "rabbitworks" --env "production" --provider "aws"` - Provisions an environment and queues a `provision` job. - Creates the environment record and assigns modules for fulfillment. ### `modules:assign` `directus hub modules:assign --env "prod-rabbit" --schemas "blog,auth"` - Attaches schema, access, and extension modules to an environment. - Validates relationships and triggers optional sync or validation jobs. ### `schema:pull` `directus hub schema:pull --env "prod-rabbit" --version "v1.2.0"` - Captures the live schema into a versioned snapshot. - Used for rollback, diffing, and environment consistency. ### `backup` `directus hub backup --env "prod-rabbit"` - Queues a backup job for database and files. - Results are logged and stored in the `backups` table upon fulfillment. ### `restore` `directus hub restore --env "dev-rabbit" --from "backup_20250726"` - Restores a prior backup into the specified environment. - Destructive by default—requires confirmation or policy flag. ### `studio:clone` `directus hub studio:clone --from "prod-rabbit" --to "dev-rabbit"` - Clones an existing environment into a new one. - Copies schema, roles, extensions, and optionally data. ### `job:run` `directus hub job:run --id "job_backup_01"` - Manually executes a pending job. - Used for testing or override; logs results to `jobs`.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 11 Job Fulfillment Jobs in the Directus Hub are discrete, declarative actions—such as provisioning a new environment, applying schema updates, or restoring from backup. When a job is scheduled (e.g., via CLI or API), it’s stored in the Hub’s `jobs` table with all necessary metadata. Execution is **intentionally decoupled** from job creation, allowing flexible fulfillment strategies across a range of infrastructures. ### 11.1 Job Lifecycle 1. **Scheduled:** A job is inserted into the system (`status: pending`) by a CLI command, UI action, or system process. 2. **Discovered:** One or more **Executors** detect eligible jobs through polling or webhook triggers. 3. **Executed:** The executor reads the job definition, performs the action, and optionally updates the Hub. 4. **Finalized:** Results, status, and logs are saved to the job record for auditing and traceability. ### 11.2 Fulfillment Strategies The system supports multiple fulfillment models depending on deployment context: - **Webhook Runner** Each environment may expose a secure webhook endpoint. When a job is scheduled, the Hub POSTs the job payload to that endpoint. The environment’s backend then executes the task (e.g., schema apply, restore). - **Internal Agent** A Directus extension (agent) running within each environment polls the Hub for jobs targeting that instance. When a job is found, the agent executes it locally and writes back results. - **External Worker** Custom services (such as GitHub Actions, Railway deploy hooks, or AWS Lambda) can poll for jobs or listen to webhook triggers. These workers use job payloads to drive scripts that provision, clone, or back up environments. - **Manual Fulfillment** Jobs can also be executed by human operators via the Directus Hub UI or CLI. The operator updates the job record manually with results and optional logs. ### 11.3 Reliability & Auditing - **Retries:** Executors can retry failed jobs based on custom logic or system policies. - **Logging:** Each job retains execution logs for observability and debugging. - **Audit Trail:** Every job tracks who or what triggered it, when, and how it resolved. - **Access Control:** Sensitive jobs (e.g., `restore`, `rebuild`) can be restricted by role or namespace. ### 11.4 Example Fulfillment Flows Below are two real-world examples of how Directus Hub jobs can be fulfilled using different infrastructure strategies:
*Figure 10.1 – Declarative vs. Imperative Fulfillment Models.* The GitHub Actions flow (left) represents a config-as-code model, where the Hub writes and triggers infrastructure pipelines. The Railway flow (right) illustrates a direct orchestration model, where jobs are fulfilled through API-based provisioning and schema application. ### 11.5 Job Record Structure ```json { "id": "job_provision_001", "action": "provision", "target": "env_rabbitworks_prod", "status": "pending", "executor": "github-actions", "params": { "schema_modules": ["schema_blog"], "access_modules": ["access_editors"], "seed_modules": ["seed_default_blog"], "extensions": ["ext_comments"] }, "log": null, "created_at": "2025-07-26T11:00:00Z" } ```

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 12. Metrics & Analytics ### **12.1 Product Usage Metrics (Internal)** These metrics help the Directus team (or host org) understand how the Hub is being used across environments and teams: - **Total Active Hubs** Number of unique Hub instances online and accessible. - **Total Active Tenants** Number of unique Tenants assigned to a studio. - **Hubs by Environment Type** Breakdown of hubs managing dev, staging, or production environments. - **Studio Count per Hub** How many studios are managed per hub, helping track complexity and growth. - **Schema Module Reuse** How often a schema module is reused across studios. High reuse = good modular design. - **Job Volume & Type** Number of jobs run per hub, broken down by type (provision, backup, restore, etc.). - **Most Common Fulfillment Methods** Whether jobs are fulfilled via GitHub Actions, agents, webhooks, or manually. - **Opt-in Telemetry Only** All metrics collection is opt-in and anonymized to respect user privacy and self-hosted installations. ### **12.2 User-Facing Analytics (Per Hub Instance)** These metrics are available to users inside their own Hub UI: - **Job History & Success Rate** Visual summary of job execution history, failures, and fulfillment times. - **Backup Frequency & Size Trends** Charts showing backup behavior and resource usage. - **Schema Drift Detection** Warnings or logs when an environment’s schema drifts from the assigned module(s). - **Access Role Coverage** Insights into unused roles, missing permissions, or access gaps. - **Audit Trails & Logs** Every significant action (provisioning, schema apply, backup, etc.) is timestamped and searchable.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 13. Cloud Strategy & Growth Opportunities **Directus Hub** enhances the Directus Cloud offering by centralizing multi-studio management, accelerating onboarding, and enabling new monetization paths—all while preserving the platform’s core commitment to user data ownership. ### 13.1 Templates & Ecosystem The Hub provides **one-click templates** with schemas, flows, roles, and sample data for real-world use cases like blogs, CRMs, and ecommerce. These templates enable: - Rapid testing and iteration - Faster onboarding and adoption - Interactive tutorials with live, working environments The built-in **marketplace** lets users discover and install official and community-contributed templates and modules—promoting reuse and expanding the Directus ecosystem. ### 13.2 Data Ownership & Portability The Hub reinforces Directus’s core principle: **your data stays yours**. - One-click backups of schema, content, and files - Transparent restore and migration between environments - No vendor lock-in—users retain full control over their infrastructure > This flexibility may increase self-hosting, but it builds trust. Pro Cloud remains the faster, easier path—not the only one. > ### 13.3 Instance Lifecycle Management Users can **create, clone, pause, and delete** studios from a single dashboard, enabling: - Prototyping and test environments - Staging/production parity - Cost control via paused instances This also supports **more accurate billing** and opens the door to flexible plans like usage-based pricing or per-studio tiers—encouraging experimentation while keeping costs predictable. ### 13.4 Self-Service Enterprise Licensing Directus Hub creates a powerful pathway for both **self-hosted** and **Directus Cloud-hosted** users to activate enterprise licensing—**without requiring sales involvement**. Because the Hub is the control layer for managing all environments, it becomes a natural interface for users to: - Deploy and manage one or many environments - Tag environments by usage, client, or billing type - **Self-subscribe to enterprise licensing directly from the Hub** Licensing can adapt based on where the environment is hosted: - **Cloud-hosted** environments (on Directus Pro Cloud) can include platform fees, usage-based scaling, and optional support tiers. - **Self-hosted** environments can activate enterprise features à la carte—enabling users to support Directus financially while still maintaining full control of their infrastructure. This lets users upgrade on their own terms while giving Directus a scalable monetization surface that works across deployment types. > Every Hub becomes a gateway for recurring revenue—aligned with the principle that your data stays yours, whether hosted or self-managed. >

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 14. Future Planning & Guardrails The MVP of the Directus Hub focuses on core orchestration, but long-term success depends on extending its capabilities in a deliberate, modular way. This section outlines key phases for growth, unresolved design questions, and technical decisions that will shape the roadmap beyond launch. ### 14.1 Implementation Considerations **Phased Approach** Rather than prescribing specific timelines, the Hub would benefit from a phased rollout: - **Foundation Phase**: Core orchestration engine, basic CLI operations, and proof of concept with GitHub Actions integration - **Ecosystem Phase**: Module system, job orchestration, and backup/restore capabilities to validate the modular architecture - **Scale Phase**: Web UI, marketplace features, and advanced tooling based on early adopter feedback ### 14.2 Key Implementation Questions - What's the minimum viable scope to validate core orchestration assumptions? - Should Hub be built as a standalone service or as a Directus extension? - How do we balance automation with manual override capabilities? - What's the right abstraction level for job executors across different infrastructures? - How do we phase the rollout to minimize risk to existing Directus users? ### 14.3 Open Technical & Product Questions Several decisions remain open and will benefit from further engineering validation or stakeholder input: - How should environment-specific extensions (e.g., dev-only tooling) be declared and enforced? - Should flows and roles be bundled inside schema modules or split into a distinct module type? - How do we validate that modules don’t reference removed or changed schema fields? - Can seed modules support non-destructive inserts based on diff logic? - What’s the right confirmation UX for destructive actions like `rebuild`? - Where should backup retention policies live—in the Hub config or delegated to providers? - How will schema drift be detected, surfaced, and remediated? ### 14.3 Design Tradeoffs & Constraints | Area | Design Decision | Tradeoff | | --- | --- | --- | | Job Execution | Use external runners (e.g. GitHub Actions, Lambda) for flexibility | Adds dependency risk; requires retries, monitoring, and manual override | | Schema Module Sharing | Allow modules to be reused across environments | Increases risk of drift or breaking changes | | Backup Strategy | Support file + DB backups with configurable retention policies | Requires storage planning and observability tooling | | Telemetry | Opt-in and anonymized by default | Limited visibility into usage trends on self-hosted Hubs | | Flows as Modules | TBD: Whether flows are a submodule of schema or standalone | Impacts module reuse and visual clarity | --- ### 14.4 Risk Analysis & Mitigation | Risk | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Users migrate off Pro Cloud using full backups | Align with open data philosophy. Make Pro Cloud a value-added choice, not a constraint. | | Schema or flow changes break production | Enforce version locking and previews before applying changes | | Job runners become misconfigured or fail | Provide retries, fallbacks, and manual overrides | | SaaS billing models create user friction | Design transparent pricing with generous free tiers |

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 15. Conclusion Directus Hub turns multi-instance complexity into a strategic advantage. It adds orchestration for schema, roles, environments, and automation—giving teams a modular, scalable way to manage Directus Studios with confidence. Whether deployed internally or used with Directus Pro Cloud, the Hub lays the foundation for version-controlled, infrastructure-aware development that aligns with modern DevOps practices—without compromising on data ownership or flexibility. By removing friction and expanding what’s possible, Directus Hub positions the platform for wider adoption across agencies, SaaS teams, and enterprise environments—unlocking new opportunities for growth, contribution, and community impact.

⬆ Back to top

--- ## 16. 👋 Feedback Welcome This proposal is intended to spark conversation. I'd love to hear your thoughts, concerns, or questions—whether you're part of the Directus team or building with the platform.

⬆ Back to top

--- **🚀 Support this Feature Request** If you find this proposal valuable, click the ⬆ upvote button on the bottom left. We need 15 votes to move it into consideration. Thanks for helping shape the future of Directus! --- If you're hiring a Product Manager who’s passionate about building great tools and developer experiences, feel free to check out my profile: [linkedin.com/in/jayshoe](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jayshoe) ⬆ Back to top

# reproduce agent enrollment + host authorization (follow-up to #797) ## Context This document builds on the `reproduce` restructuring plan agreed in #797 (Phases 1 and 2 completed in #812 and #813) and the `reproduce-windows` implementation planned for Phase 3. It defines **Phase 4 and beyond** to address two requirements: 1. **Automatic per-endpoint mTLS identity issuance and rotation** — hundreds to thousands of `reproduce-*` instances must each connect to Giganto with a unique client certificate, with automatic scheduled rotation. 2. **Per-host authorization** — each customer or environment has a limit on how many hosts it is allowed to operate; when the grant expires or is suspended, that host's connection to Giganto must be blocked immediately. This is a **design agreement document**, not an implementation plan. Once agreed, it will be split into concrete issues across the affected repositories (reproduce, aice-web-next, aimer-web, bootroot, giganto, giganto-client), and this discussion will continue to serve as the **link hub**. > **Scope boundary**: This work is **not a license management system**. Business concerns such as product sales, subscriptions, and billing are explicitly out of scope. We only define the technical permission for "is this host allowed to send data to Giganto". Throughout this document and the resulting artifacts we deliberately avoid the word "license" and use **"host authorization"** instead. When the organization eventually introduces a full license or subscription system, it will sit *above* the mechanisms defined here. > **Revision history**: This document has gone through ten rounds of structured review. Major changes accumulated so far: > > *Round 1 — initial design hardening* > > - New **"Enrollment trust model"** section with two-factor binding (MDM fingerprint or out-of-band nonce). Bundle TTL tightened to 15 minutes; re-download disabled by default. > - New **"Data governance"** section: field minimization, per-tenant redaction, retention, DSR handling, region pinning. PIPA / GDPR / CCPA / CRA framing. > - **Internet-facing `bootroot-http01-responder` is deployed as a separate instance from v1** (no shared process with the internal-services responder). Closed-network deployments may still use the single dual-mode topology. > - The authorization webhook uses **mTLS plus HMAC** (defense in depth), not HMAC alone. > - **Windows Cert Store** (`WindowsCertStore`) is a v1 key-storage option alongside PEM, not a v2 deferral. > - Phase 4a split into four sub-phases (4a-1 through 4a-4) for incremental review. > - Interface contracts (webhook JSON, `HOST_DENIED` wire format, `activation.json` schema) moved to **versioned spec files** in each affected repo. > - **Staged CA trust** added as a v2 roadmap item for zero-downtime CA rotation. > > *Round 2 — contract precision and scope honesty* > > - **Internal contradiction fixed**: `E3` and `C5` now agree. `host.expected_fingerprint` (Path A authentication factor, set at issuance time) and `host.observed_fingerprint` (drift-detection record, set on first enrollment) are explicitly distinct. > - **Wire format defined**: the second factor (Path A fingerprint or Path B nonce) is carried inside the CSR through **custom X.509 extensions under a private OID arc**, stripped by the step-ca template before signing, and read by the authorizing webhook from the parsed CSR. Exact OIDs and encoding live in `reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md` and the corresponding portal spec files. > - **Path A claim corrected**: replaced "defeats bundle theft entirely" with "raises the bar significantly". `MachineGuid` / `/etc/machine-id` / `IOPlatformUUID` are *readable values*, not cryptographic attestations. Hardware-rooted attestation via `device-attest-01` + TPM / Secure Enclave is added as an explicit v2 candidate. > - **DSR v1 hardened** with five built-in safety guards: exact match only, field whitelist, two-stage preview/execute, soft delete with 30-day grace period, and signed export archives with download audit. > - **Metadata centralization acknowledged**: the region-pinning section now explicitly distinguishes the **event data path** (region-pinned in v1) from the **portal metadata path** (centralized in v1, with field-level minimization, audit-log scrubbing, and contractual disclosure as the v1 mitigations). **Regional portal database shards** added as an explicit v2 candidate. > > *Round 3 — contract consistency and compliance posture* > > - **Webhook auth contract unified**: all references to `POST /api/authz/host` — the portal API section, the authorization webhook sequence diagram, the aimer-web section, and the step-ca provisioner description — now consistently state **mTLS plus HMAC** as the required authentication. > - **Path B fingerprint gap closed**: the wire format now specifies that the agent **always** includes its host fingerprint (OID `.1.1`) in the CSR regardless of which trust path is used. For Path A it is an authentication factor; for Path B it is recorded as `observed_fingerprint` for forensics. The per-OID role table is updated accordingly. > - **Naming inconsistency fixed**: all references to the nonce column now use `host.expected_nonce_hash` (not `expected_nonce`). > - **DSR default changed from soft delete to hard delete**: to align with GDPR Art. 17 ("without undue delay") and PIPA Art. 21 ("without delay"), DSR deletions now perform an immediate hard delete by default. A time-delayed quarantine mode is available only when the operator has activated a legal-hold or incident-recovery policy override, with the justification recorded in the audit log. > > *Round 4 — write-semantics precision* > > - **`observed_fingerprint` made set-once**: the column is now written only on the first successful enrollment (when null) and is immutable thereafter. Subsequent renewals log the current fingerprint as an `enrollment.renewal_fingerprint` audit event instead of overwriting the forensic baseline. This prevents failed attempts from polluting the value and preserves the original enrollment record for forensics. > > *Round 5 — enrollment confirmation lifecycle* > > - **Two-phase enrollment model**: webhook `{"allow": true}` is now explicitly Phase 1 (authorization only, no state mutation). Phase 2 (confirmation) fires when Giganto reports the first connection with a previously unseen cert serial, and atomically commits `cert_serial`, `observed_fingerprint`, nonce consumption, and `status = Active`. This closes the gap where a download failure after webhook allow could consume one-time credentials and lock out Path B retries. > - **Retry-safe webhook logic** for Path B: since Phase 1 does not consume the nonce, a retried finalize simply re-verifies against the still-present `expected_nonce_hash`. No special-case bypass is needed. *(Note: the initial version of this bullet described a `nonce null + cert_serial null` bypass path; Round 6 corrected this to reflect that the nonce is never consumed at webhook time.)* > - **Enrollment confirmation via Giganto GraphQL subscription**: instead of Giganto pushing HTTP to the portal, Giganto exposes a `sensorConnected` subscription and the portal subscribes over the existing mTLS GraphQL WebSocket. No new outbound networking in Giganto. A `connectedSensors` query allows catch-up after subscription drops. > - **Audit event list completed**: `enrollment.confirmed` and `enrollment.renewal_fingerprint` added to the audit event catalog. > > *Round 6 — two-phase propagation cleanup* > > - **OID role table updated**: both OIDs now explicitly state *which phase* each action belongs to. Fingerprint recording and nonce consumption happen in Phase 2, not at webhook time. > - **Retry-safe logic rewritten**: the previous formulation implied the webhook consumed the nonce and then detected the consumed state on retry. Corrected to reflect that Phase 1 never consumes the nonce — retries simply re-verify against the still-present `expected_nonce_hash`. > - **Authorization webhook diagram fixed**: portal status check changed from `host.status = Active?` to `host.status in {Enrolling, Active}?` so that initial enrollments pass validation. > - **E5 rewritten**: previously conflated "no bundle at startup" with "enrollment failure". Now distinguishes three stages: no valid bundle → `PendingActivation`; transient enrollment failure → retries in `Enrolling`; non-transient failure → `Suspended`. > > *Round 7 — stale retry-bypass cleanup* > > - **Revision history Round 5 bullet and edge-case table**: removed the obsolete "`nonce null + cert_serial null` → allow without nonce" bypass description that Round 6 had already corrected in the main body. Both now state that Phase 1 never consumes the nonce, so retries simply re-verify normally. > > *Round 8 — operational security hardening* > > - **Audit log redaction of secret material**: the CSR body and its custom-extension values (nonce, fingerprint) must never be logged in plaintext. Audit entries record only a truncated hash of the fingerprint, a `nonce_present` boolean, and the decision. This is a MUST-level spec requirement. > - **Pending enrollment lease**: the webhook now sets a pending lease when it returns `allow`, preventing concurrent ACME flows from producing duplicate certificates for the same host identity. *(Note: Round 9 later refined this to a CSR-public-key-hash-scoped lease with ACME-order-lifetime timeout, and Round 10 corrected a stale "24 hours" reference. The current design uses `pending_issuance_key_hash TEXT` + `pending_since`, not a simple boolean.)* > - **Portal availability claim corrected**: the previous "independent from portal availability" statement was wrong — cert renewal requires the authorization webhook, making the portal a hard dependency. Replaced with "partial independence" that honestly describes the data-plane independence (agent ↔ Giganto) and the control-plane dependency (renewal ↔ portal). Portal HA is now an explicit operational requirement. A signed authorization lease for offline renewal is added as a v2 candidate. > - **Suspended recovery path clarified**: removed the fictitious "portal reactivation → next renewal window" recovery option. `Suspended` is now defined as recoverable **only** through new bundle injection. The agent has no active timers or network loops in this state and cannot self-recover. > - **MSI bundle delivery clarified**: the MSI property carries a **file path** to the bundle, never the bundle content itself. Passing raw JSON on the command line would expose EAB and HMAC secrets in installer logs, Sysmon events, and MDM logs. > - **Cross-repo conformance test suite** added to Phase 4a-4: shared fixtures that exercise contract boundaries (webhook JSON, `HOST_DENIED` wire format, CSR OIDs, enrollment confirmation) run in CI for each repo. > - **`ActivationBundle.giganto_addr`** changed from `SocketAddr` to `String` (hostname:port) to align with the DNS-based endpoint model used throughout the design. > > *Round 9 — lease scoping, renewal safety, and status enum* > > - **Enrollment lease redesigned**: the lease is now scoped to the **CSR public key hash** (not the host as a whole) and **only applies during initial enrollment** (`host.status = Enrolling`). Renewals (`host.status = Active`) are exempt — a lease on renewals would cause service outages when a retry is blocked while the cert approaches expiry. Idempotent retries (same key hash) pass through the lease; only a different key hash is blocked. Lease timeout matches the **ACME order lifetime** (1–4h), not the cert lifetime (24h). Schema columns changed from `pending_issuance BOOLEAN` to `pending_issuance_key_hash TEXT`. > - **`host.status` enum unified**: both portal schemas now explicitly list `Pending | Enrolling | Active | Suspended | Revoked` in the column comment. Previously `Enrolling` was used by the webhook and Phase 2 logic but was missing from the schema definition, risking divergent implementations. > > *Round 10 — stale text cleanup* > > - **Lease timeout**: one remaining paragraph still said "24 hours"; corrected to "ACME order lifetime (typically 1–4 hours)". > - **Renewal nonce reference removed**: the renewal section previously referenced "retry against the still-valid `expected_nonce_hash`", which is self-contradictory because the nonce was already consumed at Phase 2. Replaced with a clear statement that nonce verification is not involved in renewals. ## End-to-end scenario (from the user's perspective) Deploying a Windows endpoint at a closed-network customer site via aice-web-next: 1. The customer admin signs in to their on-premises aice-web-next. 2. They select "Add host" in the UI, pick a target customer (or environment + customer in aimer-web), and download an activation bundle (`activation.json`) together with the MSI. 3. On the Windows PC, the admin runs the MSI, supplies the activation bundle, and confirms the Sysmon installation prompt. The installer then registers the reproduce-windows service. 4. On first service start, the agent performs the enrollment protocol and receives a short-lived client certificate from step-ca. 5. It begins collecting Sysmon events and streaming them to Giganto. 6. After 16 hours (2/3 of the cert lifetime) the agent renews automatically; this repeats for the life of the host. 7. When the admin suspends the host in the portal, Giganto blocks it within seconds and sends an authoritative denial to the agent; on receiving that denial the agent self-suspends (stops collecting and stops sending); step-ca then refuses the next renewal, and the current cert expires naturally shortly after. Internet customers use aimer-web with the same flow. Linux and macOS follow the same logic with different packaging. --- ## Principles - **Reuse existing organizational standards.** Keep bootroot (step-ca + OpenBao + ACME) as the CA foundation, keep aice-web-next and aimer-web as the authentication and authorization authority, and keep Giganto as the data receiver. No new CA, no new authentication stack. - **Separate mTLS authentication from host authorization.** Certificates prove *who the host is*; portal state decides *whether it is allowed to send data*. These two responsibilities must never be conflated. - **Common library first.** The three OS binaries (reproduce-windows, reproduce-linux, reproduce-macos) sit on top of common enrollment, keystore, and state-machine traits in `src/lib.rs`. Platform code is a thin adapter layer. - **Portals are OS-agnostic.** The enrollment and renewal endpoints and the `activation.json` format are OS-independent. - **Linux as the reference implementation.** While the Windows SSL.com EV certificate is being provisioned, Windows platform-specific work proceeds in parallel so that no wall-clock time is wasted. - **Environment separation** (consistent with [bootroot ARCHITECTURE.md §6.2](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#62-environment-separation)). Closed-network customers use a customer-operated step-ca; internet customers use a company-operated step-ca. CA keys and trust roots are never shared across environments. - **Short-lived certificates plus an explicit deny list.** Certificates are issued for 24 hours so that a compromised cert is usable for at most 24 hours, and when immediate blocking is required, Giganto's deny list takes effect within seconds. No CRL, no OCSP. - **Reuse ACME.** No custom enrollment protocol; use ACME with EAB. Extend bootroot's `bootroot-http01-responder` pattern to the endpoint use case. - **Respect the scope boundary.** This is a host authorization gate, not a license or subscription system. Billing, sales, renewal notifications, and similar concerns are out of scope. - **Treat the activation bundle as a high-value secret.** A leaked bundle must not by itself be enough to obtain a valid certificate. Enrollment pins the bundle to a specific host through a pre-registered fingerprint or a one-time nonce verified by the portal out-of-band. - **Minimize and govern collected data.** Endpoint telemetry from Sysmon, Falco, and osquery often carries personal data (usernames, paths, command lines, URLs). Field minimization, redaction, per-tenant retention, and data-subject request handling are first-class requirements of this design, not afterthoughts. --- ## System components ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Portal["Portal layer (authority)"] direction LR AWN["aice-web-next

This boundary is how the architecture enforces its trust zone principles. ### 1. Portal binding is permanent Once a `reproduce-*` instance is enrolled through a specific portal, it is **permanently bound** to the **step-ca + responder + Giganto** infrastructure operated by that portal. Cross-portal migration is not supported in v1. The rationale comes from [bootroot `ARCHITECTURE.md` §6.2 "Environment Separation"](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#62-environment-separation): | Environment | CA operator | Trust boundary | |---|---|---| | Closed network | customer-operated step-ca | trusted only within that closed network | | Internet | company-operated step-ca | trusted only within the internet environment | The two step-ca root certificates are **not present in each other's trust store**. As a result: - An agent enrolled through aice-web-next holds a cert signed by that closed network's step-ca, and aimer-web's Giganto will reject it during the handshake. - The reverse is equally true. - **The only way to change portals is a full reinstall**: delete the existing key and cert, inject a new `activation.json`, and re-enroll. Because portal migration is rare and automatic migration would entail a CA trust swap combined with a core key swap, the implementation and operational cost is not justified for v1. **v2 roadmap — staged CA trust**: for fleets in the thousands, full reinstall is operationally painful when the underlying concern is "rotate the CA key without disrupting data collection". The planned v2 mechanism is *staged CA trust*: Giganto temporarily trusts both the old and the new root during a transition window, agents re-enroll through the normal renewal path (which naturally picks up the new CA via `activation.json` refresh), and the old root is retired once all hosts have migrated. This does not change the "portal binding is permanent" principle — a host is still bound to a single portal — but it removes full reinstall as the only CA-rotation path. ### 2. Runtime communication boundary — the agent never talks to the portal directly After the initial `activation.json` download, the `reproduce-*` binary **makes no runtime network connection to the `aice-web-next` or `aimer-web` domain**. At runtime the agent only talks to **step-ca + responder + Giganto**: | Endpoint | When | Purpose | |---|---|---| | **step-ca directory** | Initial enrollment and every renewal (at 2/3 of the cert lifetime) | ACME `newAccount` (with EAB), `newOrder`, `finalize`, fetch cert | | **HTTP-01 responder** | On each ACME challenge | Register the validation token with scoped HMAC authentication | | **Giganto** | Continuously, starting immediately after installation | mTLS event data stream | The portal (`aice-web-next` or `aimer-web`) only appears in two paths: - **Initial provisioning**: the admin uses a browser to download the activation bundle and the agent binary, then ships them to the target host via USB, GPO, MDM, or a similar channel. The agent process itself never contacts the portal. - **Administrative actions**: the admin clicks "suspend host" in the portal UI, the portal calls the **step-ca admin API and the Giganto admin API**, and the agent **indirectly** observes the result (the next renewal is denied, a deny list entry blocks the connection, a `HOST_DENIED` response is returned). Practical benefits of this separation: 1. **Partial independence from portal availability.** If the portal goes down, agents **that already hold a valid cert** continue to collect and send data to Giganto normally — the data plane (agent ↔ Giganto) has no portal dependency. However, **cert renewal requires the portal** because step-ca calls the authorization webhook on every issuance. A portal outage therefore blocks new enrollments, admin actions, **and renewals**. The natural grace window is the remaining cert lifetime (up to 8 hours if renewal triggers at the 2/3 mark of a 24-hour cert). If the portal recovers within that window, the agent's backoff retry succeeds and no data is lost. Portal HA (high availability) deployment is therefore an operational requirement for environments that cannot tolerate an 8-hour renewal blackout. A v2 candidate — a **signed authorization lease** that step-ca can validate locally without calling the webhook — would allow renewals to proceed during brief portal outages, but is out of scope for v1. 2. **Minimal protocol surface.** The agent only needs to speak ACME (a standard) and giganto-client (already in use). With no custom portal protocol, the version-compatibility burden and the attack surface both stay small. 3. **Portal releases are independent from agent releases.** A portal code change cannot break agent compatibility, and vice versa. 4. **Clean audit boundary.** The three endpoints the agent talks to are all bootroot infrastructure (step-ca, responder) or Giganto, each with its own audit log. The portal audit log captures "admin intent"; the infrastructure audit logs capture "actual enforcement". **Implementation note — new outbound connections required in both portals:** While agents never talk to the portal at runtime, the **portals themselves** need several new outbound connections that do not exist today: | Connection | Purpose | Current state | What to add | |---|---|---|---| | Portal → **Giganto GraphQL** (subscription) | Subscribe to `sensorConnected` for Phase 2 enrollment confirmation | **Does not exist.** aice-web-next only connects to review-web's GraphQL; aimer-web does not connect to Giganto at all | New env var (`GIGANTO_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT`), new mTLS agent, **WebSocket transport** (`graphql-ws` or equivalent) for subscription support. `graphql-request` (currently used by aice-web-next) is HTTP-only and cannot do subscriptions | | Portal → **Giganto GraphQL** (mutation) | Push deny list entries | Same as above | Same client, using the mutation transport | | Portal → **step-ca admin API** | Create/delete per-host EAB credentials | **Does not exist** in either portal | New HTTP client with admin credentials (from OpenBao) | | Portal → **bootroot responder admin API** | Create/delete per-host scoped HMAC entries | **Does not exist** in either portal | New HTTP client with mTLS or AppRole auth | These connections are prerequisites for AW-3 through AW-6 (aice-web-next: host creation, webhook, subscription, and suspend/deny-list push) and AM-2 through AM-4 (aimer-web). This section defines the additional factors that pin a bundle to the specific host the admin intended. ### Threat model An attacker who obtains a freshly issued bundle (by intercepting a download, exfiltrating it from a share, etc.) could otherwise: 1. Run `reproduce-*` on an attacker-controlled machine. 2. Use the EAB credential and responder HMAC from the bundle to complete ACME enrollment. 3. Receive a valid short-lived certificate. 4. Connect to Giganto and masquerade as the intended host. The bundle's 1-hour TTL shrinks the race window but does not close it. An attacker who is fast enough, or who intercepts the bundle before the legitimate installer runs, can win the race. First-use binding (`E3`) catches the loser after the fact, but by then the attacker already holds a valid identity. ### Defense: portal-pinned host identity The portal requires an **admin-supplied host pre-registration** before issuing a bundle. At least one of the following two paths must be used; both are acceptable for v1, and the portal records which path was chosen for audit. **Path A — MDM-sourced pre-registration (preferred where MDM is in place)** 1. The admin selects the target host from an MDM inventory (Intune, Jamf, Kandji, etc.) inside the portal's "Add host" flow. 2. The portal reads the MDM-provided host identifier: Windows `MachineGuid`, Linux `/etc/machine-id`, or macOS `IOPlatformUUID`. 3. The portal records the value in `host.expected_fingerprint` and binds it to the activation token. 4. The bundle and MSI/pkg/.deb are delivered to the host through the MDM channel, not as a user download. 5. On first enrollment the agent reads the same local identifier and embeds it in the CSR through a custom extension (see "Wire format" below). The authorizing webhook extracts the value and compares it to `host.expected_fingerprint`. A mismatch returns `{"allow": false, "reason": "fingerprint_mismatch"}`. **Important caveat about Path A's strength.** `MachineGuid`, `/etc/machine-id`, and `IOPlatformUUID` are *readable values*, not *cryptographic attestations*. Any process running on the host can read them, and an attacker who at any point had access to the victim host (or to a backup or an inventory dump) can reproduce them. Path A therefore **raises the bar significantly** — an attacker must obtain both the bundle *and* the victim's fingerprint, two values that travel through completely different channels — but it is **not** the same as TPM-rooted device identity. Hardware-rooted attestation via `device-attest-01` + TPM (Windows / Linux) and Secure Enclave (macOS) is tracked as a v2 candidate. **Path B — portal-issued one-time nonce (for sites without MDM)** 1. The admin clicks "Add host" and provides the target hostname and a short description. 2. The portal generates two values: the normal activation bundle **and a short 8-character nonce** displayed only to the admin in the UI. 3. The admin delivers the bundle *and the nonce* to the host via two separate channels (e.g. the bundle via file copy, the nonce via phone, chat, or SMS to the installing operator). 4. The installer prompts for the nonce alongside the bundle path. The agent embeds the nonce in the CSR through a custom extension (see "Wire format" below). 5. The authorizing webhook extracts the nonce and verifies it against `host.expected_nonce_hash` (constant-time comparison against a stored hash). The nonce is single-use and consumed on first successful enrollment. This path requires a live out-of-band channel (phone, chat) but does not require MDM. It reduces the attack surface from "whoever can read the bundle file" to "whoever can read the bundle file AND intercepts the out-of-band nonce". ### Wire format — how the second factor reaches the webhook step-ca's authorizing webhook receives the parsed CSR as JSON. The agent's second-factor value therefore has to live **inside the CSR itself**. We carry it in **custom X.509 extensions under a private OID arc** so that the values are visible to the webhook but can be stripped from the issued certificate by the step-ca template (we do not want fingerprints or nonces baked into long-lived public artifacts). See below. ### Enrollment lifecycle: two-phase confirmation A critical subtlety: **webhook `{"allow": true}` does not mean "the agent has a cert in hand"**. Between the webhook response and the agent's successful cert installation, the following steps can still fail: ``` webhook allow → step-ca signs cert → agent downloads cert → agent stores locally → agent connects to Giganto ↑ can fail (network) ↑ can fail (disk) ``` If `observed_fingerprint` were recorded and the nonce consumed at webhook time, a download failure would leave the enrollment in a broken state: the one-time credentials are gone but the agent never received its cert. This would lock out Path B enrollments. The design therefore uses a **two-phase model**: **Phase 1 — Authorization + scoped enrollment lease (webhook time)** The webhook checks fingerprint, nonce, and host authorization status. **Lease behavior depends on the host's current state:** *Initial enrollment (`host.status = Enrolling`):* If all checks pass and no lease is currently held, the webhook sets a **scoped enrollment lease** on the host row: - `host.pending_issuance_key_hash = SHA-256(CSR public key)` — the lease is bound to a specific CSR key, not to the host as a whole. - `host.pending_since = now()` Subsequent webhook calls for the **same host** are handled as follows: | Subsequent call's CSR key hash | Lease status | Decision | |---|---|---| | Matches `pending_issuance_key_hash` | Lease held | **Allow** (idempotent retry — the agent is re-trying its own enrollment) | | Does not match | Lease held | **Deny** (`enrollment_already_in_progress` — a different key means a different ACME flow, which is the concurrent-issuance attack the lease prevents) | | Any | Lease expired | **Allow** (lease timed out; treat as a fresh attempt, re-set the lease with the new key hash) | The lease timeout is set to the **ACME order lifetime** configured in step-ca (typically 1–4 hours), not the cert lifetime (24 hours). This ensures that a failed first attempt does not block retries for longer than the order would have been valid anyway. *Renewal (`host.status = Active`):* **No enrollment lease is set or checked.** Renewals are a fundamentally different flow: the host already has a confirmed `cert_serial`, and the ACME account already exists. A duplicate renewal cert is a minor concern (two valid certs briefly overlap until the old one expires) and is far less dangerous than a service outage caused by a lease blocking a legitimate retry during the 8-hour renewal window. If a renewal webhook fails after `allow`, the agent simply retries the ACME order or cert download with backoff. Nonce verification is not involved in renewals — `expected_nonce_hash` was already consumed during the original Phase 2 confirmation and is null for any host in `Active` status. Other than the lease fields, the webhook does **not** mutate permanent host state. `observed_fingerprint`, `expected_nonce_hash`, `activation_token.used_at`, and `host.status` all remain unchanged until Phase 2. **Phase 2 — Confirmation (first Giganto connection)** When the agent connects to Giganto for the first time with its newly issued cert, Giganto observes a cert serial that is not yet recorded. Giganto exposes this as a **GraphQL subscription** event (`sensorConnected`). The portal subscribes to this subscription over the existing mTLS-authenticated GraphQL connection and receives a notification with `{ agent_name, cert_serial }`. On receiving the event, the portal atomically: 1. Sets `host.cert_serial` to the confirmed serial. 2. Sets `host.observed_fingerprint` to the fingerprint extracted during the most recent webhook call (**set-once**, only if null). 3. Clears `host.expected_nonce_hash` (Path B nonce consumed). 4. Marks `activation_token.used_at`. 5. Clears `host.pending_issuance_key_hash` and `host.pending_since` (enrollment lease released). 6. Transitions `host.status` from `Enrolling` to `Active`. 7. Logs an `enrollment.confirmed` audit event. Until Phase 2 fires, the host stays in `Enrolling` and all one-time credentials remain valid. However, the **pending enrollment lease** set in Phase 1 prevents a second concurrent ACME flow from a different key — only one issuance can be in flight at a time (idempotent retries with the same key are allowed). If the first attempt fails entirely (agent crashes, order expires, etc.), the lease times out after the **ACME order lifetime** (typically 1–4 hours), releasing the host for a fresh attempt. **Edge cases:** | Scenario | What happens | |---|---| | Webhook allows, agent downloads cert, connects to Giganto normally | Phase 2 fires within seconds. Normal path. | | Webhook allows, step-ca signs, but agent can't download (network error) | Agent retries ACME cert download (order stays valid). Lease is held but a retry with the same CSR key passes through (idempotent). No permanent state changed. | | Webhook allows, agent downloads, but can't store locally (disk error) | Agent retries storage. Lease is held. No permanent state changed. | | Webhook allows, but ACME order expires before agent downloads | Agent creates a new order with the same key pair, re-finalizes. Webhook fires again → CSR key hash matches the lease → **allowed** (idempotent retry). If the agent generates a new key pair, the hash won't match, but if the lease has timed out (ACME order lifetime, 1–4h), a fresh lease is granted. | | Agent crashes or is uninstalled after webhook allow, before Phase 2 | Lease times out after the ACME order lifetime (1–4h), then the host returns to a clean `Enrolling` state. Admin can also manually clear the lease and reissue the bundle. | | Attacker tries to use the same bundle on a different machine while the legitimate agent is enrolling | Attacker's CSR uses a different key pair → key hash does not match → lease blocks with `enrollment_already_in_progress`. | | Renewal fails after webhook allow (agent can't download new cert) | No lease was set (renewals skip the lease). Agent retries with backoff against the same step-ca order or a new one. Existing cert remains valid for the remaining 8 hours. | | Webhook allows, agent gets cert, but Giganto is unreachable | Agent stays in `Enrolling`. When Giganto becomes reachable, Phase 2 fires. Cert is valid for 24h, so there is a time limit. | | Phase 2 never fires within cert lifetime (24h) | Host stays `Enrolling`. Admin can investigate and reissue the bundle if needed. | **Giganto-side implementation:** Giganto already tracks connected sensors internally (`ingest_sensors` in `comm/ingest.rs`). On subsequent renewals the agent still includes its current fingerprint in the CSR (OID `.1.1`), but the webhook does not overwrite `observed_fingerprint`; instead it logs the value as an `enrollment.renewal_fingerprint` audit event. This preserves the original forensic record while still providing an ongoing trail of which machine is currently renewing. If the renewal fingerprint ever differs from `observed_fingerprint`, the admin can investigate whether the host was reimaged, the bundle was sideloaded onto a different machine, or the identity was compromised. ### Bundle TTL and re-download policy — tightened To limit the race window further: - TTL is reduced to **15 minutes** (down from 1 hour) for the bundle itself. - Re-download is **disabled by default**. If the admin needs to re-download, they must explicitly click "Reissue bundle", which generates a new EAB, new responder HMAC kid, and a new nonce (Path B) or re-reads the MDM fingerprint (Path A). - A bundle that has been re-downloaded once is marked `superseded` and cannot be used even if the original file still exists somewhere. ### Bundle contents — factor separation `activation.json` intentionally does **not** contain the MDM fingerprint (Path A) or the nonce (Path B). Those are held by the host's hardware or the admin's out-of-band channel. This makes the bundle useless on its own even if intercepted. ### Summary | Factor | Held by | How it is delivered to the agent | How the portal verifies | |---|---|---|---| | EAB credential | activation bundle | bundle file | step-ca consumes on `newAccount` | | Responder HMAC | activation bundle | bundle file | bootroot responder verifies | | Host fingerprint (Path A) | host hardware | read locally by the agent | authorizing webhook compares to `host.expected_fingerprint` | | One-time nonce (Path B) | admin, out-of-band | admin enters during installation | authorizing webhook hashes and compares to `host.expected_nonce_hash` (constant-time, KDF), single-use | A single stolen factor cannot produce a valid cert. Both the bundle **and** either a matching hardware identifier or an intercepted out-of-band nonce are required. --- ## Activation bundle `activation.json` ### Schema ```json { "version": "1", "issued_at": "2026-04-11T14:30:00Z", "expires_at": "2026-04-11T14:45:00Z", "host_id": "01HP5NXQ...", "san_identifier": "01HP5NXQ.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com", "agent_name": "01HP5NXQ", "kind": "sysmon", "grant_scope": { "kind": "environment_customer", "aice_id": "env-prod-kr", "customer_id": "cust-division-a" }, "trust_model": { "second_factor": "mdm_fingerprint" }, "step_ca": { "directory": "https://step-ca.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com/acme/endpoints/directory", "ca_root_pem": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n..." }, "eab": { "kid": "eab_01HP5...", "hmac_b64": "..." }, "responder": { "url": "https://responder.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com", "hmac_kid": "hmac_01HP5...", "hmac_secret_b64": "..." }, "giganto": { "addr": "giganto.aimer.aicers.com:38370", "server_name": "giganto.aimer.aicers.com" } } ``` Note: `trust_model.second_factor` tells the agent which second factor to collect at enrollment time. `"mdm_fingerprint"` = Path A (read local hardware ID), `"nonce"` = Path B (prompt the installing admin). The bundle never contains the actual fingerprint or nonce value. ### Delivery and lifetime - Downloadable only through an authenticated portal session. - TTL of **15 minutes** from issuance. A bundle past its TTL is unusable even if copied elsewhere. - **Re-download is disabled by default.** If the admin needs another copy, they must explicitly click "Reissue bundle", which invalidates the previous bundle and all its credentials (new EAB, new responder HMAC kid, new nonce or re-read MDM fingerprint). - Once the bundle is used for a successful enrollment, the portal marks it as consumed and it cannot be reused. - The agent also deletes the file after a successful enrollment to prevent reuse. - MDM-based deployment: Windows via an MSI property that specifies a **file path** (e.g. `BUNDLE_PATH=C:\path\to\activation.json`), **never the bundle content itself** — command-line arguments appear in Windows Installer logs, Sysmon `ProcessCreate` events, and MDM deployment logs, so passing the raw JSON (which contains EAB and HMAC secrets) on the command line would expose them. Linux via a file placed at `/etc/reproduce/activation.json`. macOS via the pkg payload. In all MDM scenarios, Path A of the enrollment trust model is strongly recommended so that the bundle and the host fingerprint are never in the same channel. ### Security properties - The EAB credential and the responder HMAC are **two distinct credentials** with separate signing contexts, so a compromise of one does not breach the other. - The responder HMAC is **scoped per host**, so it cannot register tokens for any identifier other than the one assigned to that host. - The EAB credential is single-use. After the first ACME `newAccount` call, step-ca retires it. - The bundle **does not contain the second factor** (neither the MDM fingerprint nor the out-of-band nonce). A leaked bundle on its own cannot complete enrollment. See "Enrollment trust model" above. --- ## Enrollment and renewal flow ### First enrollment (sequence) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as reproduce-* participant R as responder participant C as step-ca participant P as portal participant G as Giganto Note over A: startup: parse bundle,

The responder HMAC is not rotated on renewal. - After the challenge succeeds, the agent submits `finalize`. - **Before signing, step-ca calls the portal's authorizing webhook** (see "Authorization webhook" below) to re-check whether the host is still authorized. The webhook receives the requested identifier and returns `{"allow": true}` or `{"allow": false, "reason": "..."}`. - If the webhook allows, step-ca issues the new cert, the agent fetches it, and `KeyStore::rotate()` performs an atomic swap. - If the webhook denies, step-ca rejects the finalize step with an ACME error. The agent receives `EnrollmentError::Denied` and stays in `Running` for as long as the existing cert is still valid. ### Authorization webhook — how step-ca asks the portal The portal is the authoritative source for host authorization; step-ca itself has no knowledge of which hosts are still allowed. The link between the two is a **step-ca `AUTHORIZING` webhook** configured on the `endpoints` provisioner. Flow on every issuance (initial enrollment and every renewal): ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as agent participant C as step-ca participant P as portal A->>C: finalize(CSR, identifier = host-id.endpoints.) (EnrollmentError::Denied on the agent side) end ``` Key properties of the webhook: - **Defense in depth: HMAC plus mTLS**. Step-ca signs every webhook request with a shared secret stored in OpenBao, and the underlying HTTPS transport uses **mTLS between step-ca and the portal** (step-ca presents the certificate issued by its own internal-services provisioner; the portal pins that certificate's issuer). HMAC alone would suffice for authentication, but combining it with mTLS localizes the trust surface: even if the HMAC secret leaks, an attacker still needs a valid client certificate from the internal services CA to reach the endpoint at all. The portal rejects any call that fails either check. - **Stateless from step-ca's side**: step-ca keeps no host allow/deny list of its own. Every decision goes back to the portal, which is the single source of truth. - **Immediate effect**: once the admin flips `host.status` in the portal database, the next webhook invocation (i.e. the next renewal attempt for that host) sees the change.
