Treating this as "just security logs" would expose the organization to unnecessary regulatory and customer-trust risk. Data governance is therefore a first-class part of this design, not an afterthought. The design addresses five concerns: minimization, redaction, retention, data-subject request handling, and region pinning. Each is scoped to what is realistically deliverable in v1; more advanced controls are noted as v2 candidates. ### Legal and regulatory framing Concrete obligations depend on where the data is collected and where it is stored: - **Korea PIPA**: minimization of collection (Art. 16), purpose limitation (Art. 18), safe handling (Art. 29), destruction after retention period (Art. 21), controls on cross-border transfer (Art. 28-8, 28-9). - **EU GDPR**: lawful basis (Art. 6), minimization and purpose limitation (Art. 5), data subject rights (Art. 15–22), DPIA when systematic monitoring of employees is involved (Art. 35), international transfer mechanisms (Chapter V). - **EU CRA**: technical documentation, support period, vulnerability handling, and risk assessment obligations for products placed on the EU market (effective 2024-12-10, full application 2027-12-11). - **California CCPA/CPRA**: employee data has been in scope since the 2023-01-01 expiry of the employee exemption. - **United States (sectoral)**: HIPAA if any covered health data is captured; GLBA for financial institutions. This design does not attempt to be "PIPA-compliant" or "GDPR-compliant" on its own — compliance is determined by the full deployment context. What it does is provide the technical primitives that a compliant deployment requires: a place to apply minimization, a hook to apply redaction, a knob to set retention, and a path for data-subject requests to reach the data. ### 1. Field minimization (v1 required) Not every Sysmon/Falco/osquery field is sent to Giganto. A per-kind **field allowlist** is maintained in the `reproduce` repo under `configs/field-allowlists/`, one file per `RawEventKind`. Fields not on the allowlist are dropped by the Collector *before* serialization, so they never leave the host. Examples of fields that are explicitly **not** on the default allowlist: - Sysmon `CommandLine` full text (only the executable path is on the list; the full command-line becomes opt-in via `kind: sysmon_full_cmdline`) - Sysmon `User` raw principal name (only a hashed form) - Falco `proc.cmdline`, `fd.name` for user-space paths under `/home` - osquery `processes.cmdline`, `process_open_files.path` under user home directories The allowlist is versioned alongside the code, reviewed by the security team on every change, and shipped as part of the `reproduce-*` binary. Changing the allowlist is a code change, not a runtime config change, so customer operators cannot silently widen the scope. ### 2. Per-tenant redaction (v2 — deferred) In v1, field minimization is handled entirely at the agent side (see §1 above). Giganto receives only the fields that passed the agent-side allowlist and stores them as-is. No Giganto-side redaction is applied. In v2, customers will be able to configure additional redaction rules per tenant (regex masking, allowlist overrides, path shortening) via an `ingest_policy` table managed by the portal and pushed to Giganto. Redaction would be applied at Giganto ingest time, enabling per-customer rules that evolve independently of agent releases. This is deferred to v2 because it requires Giganto to gain per-tenant awareness in its storage layer — a significant structural change to a system that currently stores all events in a shared RocksDB with a single global retention policy. ### 3. Retention (v1 — Giganto's existing global retention; per-tenant retention in v2) Giganto already has a global retention mechanism (`retain_periodically()`, default 100 days, configurable per deployment). In v1, this existing mechanism is used as-is — all events share the same retention period regardless of tenant. Per-tenant retention (different TTLs per customer or environment) is deferred to v2 because Giganto's current RocksDB storage is not partitioned by tenant. Adding per-tenant retention requires either per-tenant column families, a tenant-aware key prefix scheme, or a secondary index — all of which are significant storage-layer changes. For v1 compliance purposes, the global retention period should be set to the **shortest** required by any tenant's policy. Customer DPAs should document the global retention value. ### 4. Data-subject requests (v2 — deferred) PIPA and GDPR both require that individuals can request access to, correction of, or deletion of data about them. Because endpoint telemetry is attributed to *hosts*, not *users*, honoring such a request requires tracing from a user identifier through the events that reference it, which in turn requires Giganto to support per-field querying and targeted deletion — capabilities it does not have today. DSR execution is deferred to v2 in its entirety. When implemented, the design will include: - Exact-match-only search on a whitelisted set of identifier fields - Two-stage workflow with preview before execution - Hard delete by default (GDPR Art. 17 "without undue delay", PIPA Art. 21 "without delay"); quarantine only with an explicit legal-hold override - Export auditing with signed archives - Per-tenant job tracking For v1, the agent-side field allowlist (§1) serves as the primary mitigation: fields most likely to carry personal data (`command_line`, `user`, paths under `/home/`) can be excluded from collection entirely, so that DSR requests against those fields have no matching data in Giganto. If a DSR request arises before v2 is ready, the operator must handle it manually using Giganto's existing data export and RocksDB-level tooling. ### 5. Region pinning and cross-border transfer (v1 required for aimer-web) aimer-web is internet-facing and may collect data from customers in jurisdictions that restrict cross-border transfer (EU, Korea, China, etc.). Each aimer-web Environment has a **region** attribute (`environment.region`), which determines: - Which Giganto instance receives the events (regional Giganto deployment). - Which step-ca instance signs the certificates (regional CA). - Which `bootroot-http01-responder` instance handles the ACME validation. v1 ships with at least one region; additional regions are deployed as customer demand requires. An Environment cannot move across regions without a full re-enrollment of its hosts (consistent with the "portal binding is permanent" principle). aice-web-next is closed-network and all infrastructure lives inside the customer's own environment, so cross-border transfer does not apply by construction — the customer's own PIPA/GDPR obligations determine the placement. #### Metadata centralization — explicit acknowledgement Region pinning above only covers the **event data path** (Sysmon/Falco/osquery telemetry → Giganto). The **portal metadata path** is handled separately and currently centralized: - The portal database (aice-web-next or aimer-web) holds host UUIDs, host display names, customer- or admin-supplied descriptions, audit trails of admin actions, activation token issuance records, DSR job records, and observed/expected fingerprints. - This metadata is **itself personal data** in many jurisdictions: a host display name and an admin description routinely identify a specific employee or device. - In v1, aimer-web's portal database is **centralized**, not regionalized. That means metadata for an EU-region or Korea-region Environment may be stored on infrastructure outside that region. This is a deliberate v1 trade-off, not an oversight. v1 mitigates the risk in three ways: 1. **Field minimization at the portal level.** The portal restricts free-text fields: `host.description` is capped at a short length, and the UI guidance steers admins away from putting personal names in it. The host display name field is similarly restricted. Customer-supplied free text is the smallest possible footprint. 2. **Audit log scrubbing.** Audit log entries record actor account IDs (opaque UUIDs), not personal names, wherever possible. Where a personal name leaks in (for example an admin's display name), the audit row carries it; this is acceptable because admin identities are inside the operating organization, not the customer's data subjects. 3. **Contractual disclosure.** Customer Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) must explicitly state that portal metadata is centralized in the operator's region, list which fields cross borders, and identify the basis for transfer (SCCs, adequacy, etc.). This is a customer-contract obligation that goes hand in hand with the technical setup. A **regional portal database shard** — splitting the portal database itself by region so that metadata for an EU customer never leaves the EU — is a v2 candidate. It is not in v1 because it requires the portal application to become region-aware throughout (login routing, audit aggregation, cross-shard queries), which is a much larger change than the host-authorization scope of this work. aice-web-next is not affected: it runs entirely inside the customer's closed network, so its portal metadata never leaves that network in the first place. ### 6. Audit, DPIA, and customer-facing documentation - **Audit logging (v1)** — changes to the agent-side field allowlist configuration are tracked via code review (the allowlist is versioned in the reproduce repo). In v2, when Giganto gains per-tenant `ingest_policy`, every change to an `ingest_policy` row will be logged in `audit_db` with actor, timestamp, and before/after values. - **DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment)** — deployments that involve systematic monitoring of employees must run a DPIA under GDPR Art. 35. This design does not conduct the DPIA; it provides the documentation, data flows, and configuration surface that the DPIA requires as input. - **Customer-facing privacy documentation** — the default field allowlist and the global retention period are published in customer documentation so that customers can include them in their own privacy notices. Per-tenant redaction capabilities will be documented when available in v2. ### v2 / out of scope - **Giganto per-tenant data governance engine** — per-tenant redaction at ingest time, per-tenant retention TTL, DSR execution engine (search, delete, export). Requires Giganto to gain tenant-aware storage (currently single shared RocksDB with global retention). This is the single largest v2 item. - **Pseudonymization of user identifiers** at ingest (stable hash + separate lookup table) — defers to v2 because it affects detection-rule authoring. - **Field-level encryption at rest** per tenant — v2. - **Automatic detection of new sensitive fields** in future Sysmon/Falco/osquery versions — v2. ### Scope boundary restated This section defines *what reproduce-\* and the portals will do*. It does not: - Determine whether any specific deployment is legally compliant (that is the customer's obligation with their own DPO/legal counsel). - Replace the need for a DPIA or a PIPA privacy impact assessment in the deployments that require them. - Cover contractual issues (data processing agreements, sub-processor lists, customer contracts). What it does guarantee is that the **foundational compliance primitive** is present from v1: **agent-side field minimization** (data that is never collected cannot be a compliance liability) plus Giganto's existing global retention. Per-tenant redaction, per-tenant retention, and DSR execution are v2 items that build on top of this foundation once Giganto gains tenant-aware storage. Region pinning of event data is v1 for aimer-web deployments. --- ## Platform-specific `reproduce-*` implementation ### Common structure Structure shared by all three binaries: - All of them reuse the common-library traits (`EnrollmentClient`, `KeyStore`, `Controller`, `AgentState`). - Each `main.rs` is a thin layer that assembles `load config → initialize KeyStore → run Enrollment (or load existing Identity) → Controller::run`. - Service-manager integration lives in a per-OS adapter (`service.rs`, `systemd.rs`, `launchd.rs`). - Log sinks are per-OS (`tracing-eventlog`, `tracing-journald`, or an `os_log` wrapper). ### reproduce-windows - **Collection**: Sysmon (Operational channel) — EventLogCollector (#797 Phase 3) - **Service**: Windows Service Control Manager (`windows-service` crate) - **Logs**: Windows Event Log (`tracing-eventlog` or ETW) - **Packaging**: MSI via WiX v4 - **Signing**: SSL.com EV + eSigner - **Host fingerprint**: `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid` - **Key storage**: two backends available from v1 — `WindowsCertStore` (LocalMachine\\My, preferred for production) and PEM files with service-account-only ACL (`icacls`, used when the Cert Store is not available). Giganto-side ingest-time redaction and per-tenant retention are v2 - **Phase 4b — Windows platform-specific work (in parallel with 4a)** - Complete EventLogCollector - Windows Service adapter (SCM) - Windows Event Log tracing sink - Windows host fingerprint, ACL-based key storage - MSI (WiX v4) project, activation bundle input UI, Sysmon bundle - CI build (unsigned) - **Phase 5 — Windows integration** - After the Phase 4a common library stabilizes, combine with reproduce-windows - End-to-end verification in an internal test environment using the unsigned MSI - **Phase 6 — Windows production signing + pilot** - SSL.com EV certificate and eSigner integration (CI) - Signed MSI distribution - Initial customer pilot - **Phase 7 — macOS port** - reproduce-macos scaffold - OsqueryCollector (reusing the one built in Phase 4) - launchd adapter, pkg packaging, notarization pipeline - Apple Developer Program registration (prerequisite work) - **Phase 8 — Linux osquery addition** - Add OsqueryCollector alongside Phase 3's Falco collector - reproduce-linux gains the ability to pick Falco or osquery --- ## Prerequisite work (external dependencies) These are the prerequisites for starting Phase 4. Every item runs **in parallel**, and given the lead times involved, all of them should be started within the organization immediately. ### Organizational and procurement tasks (start in parallel) 1. **Obtain a D-U-N-S number** — apply through Korean Dun & Bradstreet. This is a **prerequisite for both the Windows EV certificate and the macOS Apple Developer Program**, and must be started first. 2. **Request SSL.com EV + eSigner** — starts once the D-U-N-S number is in hand. Two to three weeks to issuance. 3. **Apple Developer Program (Organization enrollment)** — starts once the D-U-N-S number is in hand. One to four weeks to approval. 4. **Build the Linux deb signing infrastructure from scratch** — GPG key creation, repo hosting, and a CI signing pipeline. Not urgent; can proceed in parallel after the Windows work begins. 5. **Coordinate with the bootroot team** — secure organizational agreement on the scoped HMAC mode extension and its delivery schedule. ### Separate prerequisite issues (one per repo) 6. **bootroot#N** — add a scoped HMAC mode to the responder (Plan A+). 7. **giganto-client#N** — add the `HOST_DENIED` response type. Must be merged before the Giganto work, since Giganto depends on the type. 8. **giganto#N** — host authorization enforcement (SAN verification, deny list, admin API, and sending `HOST_DENIED`). 9. **aice-web-next#N** — host authorization data model, API, and UI. 10. **aimer-web#N** — host authorization (two-tier allocation) data model, API, and UI. Once agreement is reached, each of these will be tracked as a **stub discussion** in its respective repo — linking back here and summarizing the scope for that repo — and then split into implementation issues. --- ## Open questions All design-level decisions have been settled. What remains are details that will be resolved naturally during implementation. - **Responder domain naming** — the actual `*.endpoints.` DNS zones for closed-network and internet environments are an operator decision. - **Rust ACME client choice** — `instant-acme` is the leading candidate (pending verification of its EAB support); to be finalized when implementation begins. - **Per-host HMAC kid format** — whether to use a ULID with a prefix or a different scheme is an implementation detail. - **Cert lifetime tuning** — the v1 default is 24 hours, but it can be adjusted to 12h, 48h, or 72h based on operational experience. ### v2 candidates (out of scope, future decisions) - **Hardware-rooted device identity (`device-attest-01` + TPM / Secure Enclave)** — replaces the Path A "stable hardware identifier" approach with cryptographic attestation. Requires that step-ca's open-source `device-attest-01` flow becomes end-to-end usable, and that TPM 2.0 / Secure Enclave is available on the target hosts. Where available, this elevates Path A from "raises the bar" to "cryptographically rooted" and is the proper long-term answer to the bundle-theft threat model. - **macOS Endpoint Security framework collector** — requires entitlement application and a System Extension implementation. - **Linux / macOS native key backends** — kernel keyring, macOS Keychain. Windows Cert Store ships in v1; the others follow. - **Staged CA trust for zero-downtime CA rotation** — Giganto trusts both the old and the new root during a migration window so that a fleet can rotate its CA without per-host reinstall. See "Portal binding is permanent" for context. - **Signed authorization lease for offline renewal** — the portal pre-issues a short-lived signed token (e.g. a JWT with the host's authorization state, valid for N hours) that step-ca can validate locally without calling the webhook. This would allow cert renewals to proceed during brief portal outages, removing the hard portal dependency for renewals noted in the "Partial independence from portal availability" section. - **Advanced data-subject-request workflow** — self-service request intake, automated 30-day deadline tracking, region-scoped execution. - **Pseudonymization at ingest** — stable hash of user identifiers with a separate lookup table. - **Field-level encryption at rest per tenant**. - **Regional portal database shards** — splits the portal metadata store by region so that metadata for an EU or Korea customer never leaves its region. Requires the portal application (login routing, audit aggregation, cross-shard queries) to become region-aware. Pairs with the v1 region-pinning of event data described in "Data governance §5". - **A-double topology for closed-network deployments** — closed-network operators who want audit-level segmentation can move to the same two-instance topology used by internet-facing deployments. - **CRL or OCSP** — only needed if additional cert verifiers appear alongside Giganto. - **Air-gapped deployment** — an offline enrollment protocol plus manual bundle delivery. --- ## References ### Prior discussions / issues - aicers/reproduce#797 — reproduce restructuring + reproduce-windows implementation plan (the source for this work) - aicers/reproduce#812 — Phase 1: `[lib] + [[bin]]` restructuring ✅ - aicers/reproduce#813 — Phase 2: controller/collector commonization ✅ ### External documents - bootroot `ARCHITECTURE.md` — the PKI foundation for this work: - [§5 System Authentication Model](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#5-system-authentication-model) — the existing table of mTLS connections inside the organization; `reproduce-* → Giganto (mTLS)` is the new row this work adds - [§6.2 Environment Separation](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#62-environment-separation) — closed-network vs internet CA split, trust roots never shared - [§7.1 ACME as the Primary Mechanism](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#71-acme-as-the-primary-mechanism) — ACME as the standard issuance protocol - [§8 Certificate Lifetime and Rotation](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#8-certificate-lifetime-and-rotation) — short-lived certs and automatic rotation - [bootroot `DESIGN.md`](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/DESIGN.md) — certificate rotation, secret management, automation boundaries - aice-web-next `decisions/account-management.md` — customer / role / customer_db structure - aimer-web `docs/en/environment-management.md` — Environment and Trust Registry - Smallstep official docs: - https://smallstep.com/docs/step-ca/acme-basics/ - https://smallstep.com/docs/step-ca/provisioners/ - https://smallstep.com/blog/acme-eab-overview/ - [smallstep/certificates#650 — ACME External Account Binding (merged 2022-01-31)](https://github.com/smallstep/certificates/pull/650) ### External crate candidates - `instant-acme` — Rust ACME client - `windows-service` — Windows Service integration - `rcgen` — CSR generation - `rustls`, `quinn` — mTLS (already in use) - `tracing-eventlog`, `tracing-journald` — per-platform log sinks --- ## The role of this discussion This discussion is the **canonical source for rationale and design decisions**. It is intentionally *not* the canonical source for interface contracts. The distinction matters: | Artifact | Lives in | Versioned how | Example | |---|---|---|---| | Rationale, trade-offs, accepted decisions | This discussion (#846) | Prose, with edit history | "We chose HTTP-01 + bootroot responder because…" | | **Interface contracts** | **Spec files in each affected repo**, committed alongside the implementing code | Semver, with review | `activation.json` schema, `HOST_DENIED` wire format, authorization webhook JSON | Concretely, each of the following will have a versioned spec file in its home repo once the interface is ready to implement: - `reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md` — `activation.json` schema, TTL, trust model references - `reproduce/specs/agent-state.md` — the state machine transitions and the events that drive them - `giganto-client/specs/host-denied.md` — `HOST_DENIED` message layout, reason codes - `giganto/specs/deny-list.md` — deny list GraphQL mutations, query, and storage semantics - `giganto/specs/enrollment-confirmation.md` — `sensorConnected` subscription schema and `connectedSensors` query for Phase 2 enrollment confirmation - `aice-web-next/specs/authz-webhook.md` and `aimer-web/specs/authz-webhook.md` — the step-ca authorizing webhook contract, identical between the two portals - `bootroot/specs/scoped-hmac.md` — the scoped HMAC registration API Changes to a spec file require a code review in its own repo and a reference back to an updated section of this discussion if the rationale has changed. This keeps discussion prose from becoming the single point of failure for cross-repo compatibility. Once the design is agreed, work proceeds as follows: 1. Finalize this discussion as the agreed version of the rationale. 2. Register stub discussions or issues in each repo (bootroot, giganto, giganto-client, aice-web-next, aimer-web), each linking back here. 3. Draft the initial spec files in each repo as part of Phase 4a-1. 4. Finalize repo-specific details through reviews with the relevant owners. 5. Start the organizational prerequisites in parallel (D-U-N-S, SSL.com EV, Apple Developer Program, Linux deb infrastructure). 6. In the reproduce repo, begin Phase 4a-1 through 4a-4 followed by 4b once Phase 3 is complete. 7. This discussion lives on as a link hub — rationale here, contracts in the spec files, code in the implementing PRs. Review and feedback are welcome. In particular, we'd like input on: - **Cross-portal schema compatibility** — whether the API contract of the two-tier allocation model stays aligned between aice-web-next and aimer-web. - **bootroot responder scoped HMAC mode extension** — whether the bootroot team can accept this direction, and any alternatives worth considering. - **Giganto host authorization enforcement** — the SAN format, the deny list lifetime policy, and the details of the `HOST_DENIED` protocol. - **Phase 4a/4b parallelism** — how to reach early agreement on the trait signatures needed to unblock the Windows track while the Linux reference is still in flight.

nodes.title: Deploying migrations and perform seeding on multi tenants database
nodes.body:

nodes.title: Ability to reload AWSOptions after ASP.NET Core Lambda Startup
nodes.body:
## The Question
I am enhancing an existing ASP.NET Core Lambda solution to add multi-tenant support.  Our multitenant setup would use the same codebase (front-end, ANguar, oaded from S3 buckets and back-end, .NET Lambdas) but separate database (either by schema, physical database or physical cluster - depnding on the client).

Per tenant requests would be recognized by incoming host since each client would have their own domain (or be mapped to one of our tenant-specific subdomains).  Configuration for our application resides in AWS Parameter Store and would be composed of a Common section (/myapplication/Commmon) which would contain mappings between Hosts and Logical Tenant Names. In addition, there would be tenant-specific sections, for each configured tenant, that would contain tenant-specific application configuration values (/myapplication/tenantA/, /myapplication/tenantB/). 

Processing piepeline in the ASP.NET Core 3.1 application would contain custom middleware which would do the initial mapping of Host to Tenant and then load the appropriate tenant specific configuration section.
I have tried it out in a local environment and al works great.  Next step is to install in in AWS and make it work which I doubt should be an issue.

One problem I have noticed is that AWSOptions are loaded in the ConfigureServices section of my ASP.NET Core app while our middleware does not run until the next Configure section.  AWSOptions are loaded from "the base" configuration "key (e.g. /myapplication/AWS/UserPoolClientId) and while I have tried to reload it from a tenant-specific section using this construct:

configuration.Bind($"{tenantName}:AWS", awsOptions.Value);

But it does not seem to work.

My general question is whether there is a way to reload AWSOptions to support different Congito (and other AWS service) on a per-client/tenant basis rather than relying on the AWSOptions configured at the "base" level.  Alternatively, is there a way to lazily configure Congito (or other AWS Services) to delay configuration until the client is known.

### Environment

- Build Version: 2.2.2
- OS Info: Compiled on Ubuntu 20.04, runtime set to linux-x64
- Build Environment: Azure pipelines (pool Ubuntu 20.04, runtime set to linux-x64)
- Targeted .NET Platform: ASP.NET Core 3.1


---

This is a :question: general question

nodes.title: Best strategy for a single, shared tenant-aware database and centrally-controlled data access?
nodes.body:
Related #7455

## TLDR / Summary

I am taking an old homebrew proprietary multitenant CMS with a single database per environment and porting it to OC CMS. In the original, tenants' data is stored, tracked, managed, and controlled from a central admin UI. Each tenant sees users/content/etc. as though they were their own data. In reality, creating something stores it centrally and maps it as coming from the tenant (the central system has final authority). Each tenant/user combo then queries the central system that responds by dictating what data should be exposed/presented to the tenant/user. What is the safest and most maintainable way of doing this in OC CMS? I'm thinking it would involve wrapping the existing `ISession` instance with a custom class that controls how queries are done. Is this safe? If so, how likely is it that core WILL NOT break it with a future update? Does this warrant an Issue to modify core in any way to keep such a strategy secure/safe? (Questions re-iterated at bottom)

## Problems

As much as possible, I want to minimize customization of the OrchardCMS/OrchardCore codebase's default behavior (to avoid needing to maintain alternate code). Thus far, I've been following the approach recommended in #7455 where each tenant has its own YesSql collection, and data is remotely accessed across tenants using ShellHost/ShellScope. This has presented a number of problems though (listed below).

The common thread is that this approach results in additional code complexity, long-term maintenance, inefficient scaling, and a bad developer experience. We are now looking into single-database alternatives that preserve the flexible configuration allowed for each OC tenant (features, theme, sub-routed admin, etc.).

### **Tenant-Scoped Data**

#### **Users**

I use AzureAD for auth, but each user has to link it to a local user in each tenant. When moving from one tenant to another, users have to log in each time rather than already being authenticated. I'd like the user to already be authenticated everywhere at once and let authorization handle tenant-scoping of the UI (e.g. what users are displayed as part of a tenant, etc.).

#### **Content**

If a tenant marks that content is allowed to be shared/visible (read-only), I'd either have to constantly sync data between tenants' tables with BackgroundTasks/IContentManager.ImportAsync or use faux reference items that need their own custom logic and can become invalid "null" holes. Both strategies introduce unnecessary complexity and points of failure.

#### **Other**

For everything else, we will likely run into similar problems as Content, but without the built-in utility to migrate/import across YesSql containers (like WorkflowTypes). Would need to devise custom solutions for each type to individually choose data should be exposed and to where.

### **Omni-Tenant Operations**

I'm worried about performance and complexity at scale when dealing with omni-tenant operations. If 1) I have hundreds of tenants, 2) I need to do many regular/recurring operations with all of them, and 3) each operation requires multiple SQL queries, then I will need to repeat all of these queries/operations in a loop through all tenants and aggregate/resolve the data. Even if I manually compose a single SQL query instead, I'd likely be joining together hundreds or thousands of tables. It would be much simpler to just grab all the data from a single source directly and do what's needed without any additional work.

An alternative we thought of is to use a "shared" tenant, push copies of data there, and then use that for aggregate tasks, but it has issues of its own (can't "write" to the central data for en masse changes, adds unnecessary points of failure with desyncs, more code complexity, and lots of custom code to maintain, etc.)

### **DB Complexity**

Even with the few experimental tenants that have been made so far, looking at the database shows that it's become a gigantic mess of tables. Things are hard to find, data is spread out everywhere, etc. The old CMS database is much simpler, streamlined, and easier to maintain.

## Possible Solution

What if I replace the service registration for `IStore` with a derived class that overrides the `CreateSession()` method so that it returns a custom implementation, e.g. a `CentralizedSession`?

### Concept

The new session internally creates an instance of `YesSql.Session` and lets it do most of the work as normal. But, when creating IQuery instances via `Query`/`QueryIndex`, it could pre-emptively start with a ReduceIndex that groups any given document by tenant name (using the `ShellScope.Current.ShellContext.Settings.Name`) and then call the intended `Query`/`QueryIndex` before returning it.

Would also need to ensure that tenants don't activate features without first running their DataMigrations on the Default tenant, but that doesn't seem dangerous or too difficult.

### Risks

The most dangerous/hacky aspect of this solution is the fact that OC modules have the potential to directly execute SQL statements against their respective databases (which could then violate the central session's control over things).

The only example of this I can find though in the OC source code is the `IndexingTaskManager` implementation. From what I can tell, it just keeps track of the latest "update"/"delete" status of ContentItemIds in the system. *Seems* like it wouldn't be harmful to this setup, but these index tasks are used by the `LuceneIndexingService` which could have other repercussions. It seems like a search engine API for data stored in ContentItems (I think?), so there might be a risk of one tenant's search accidentally pulling up links to content in other tenants inadvertently. Not sure yet.

Still, that doesn't mean that other OC features in the future won't rely on direct SQL statements.

## Questions

1. Do you foresee any other risks with this approach and do you think it is safe to move forward this way?
2. Is there any way to guarantee such an approach could work long-term? For example, are there existing similar use cases that the OC CMS maintainers are making sure not to compromise with future updates?
3. If there is a concrete way this design intent could be integrated into the configuration of a SaaS OC CMS app in the core repo, then should an Issue be opened?
